#5797. 1968 Mustang GT500KR For Sale With 60,000 Miles Shown Has 428 Cobra Jet V8 And Shelby Signature

If you missed the boat on this uniquely specced 1969 Shelby GT500, fret not, for Bring a Trailer has a 1968 GT500KR (King of the Road) up for grabs, with an odometer reading of 60,000 miles and a bid price currently sitting at $77,777. Featuring a 428-cubic-inch Cobra Jet V8 and finished in Wimbledon White with blue stripes, this GT500 is one of 1,053 KR fastbacks produced between April and July 1968. The Cobra Jet is paired with a four-speed manual, making this one of 530 four-speed KR fastbacks. Sure, Carroll Shelby made a lot of cool cars, but the fact that this GT500 also has the legend's signature on the dash panel takes the specialty factor even further.

The reproduction data plate reveals the GT500KR was indeed a Wimbledon White example from the factory, and the blue stripes were added later by a previous owner. The description also mentions that the original owner used to race the car and that it has a replacement engine block, said to have been installed during the late 1960s. This Shelby comes with power steering, power front disc brakes, and a 3.50:1 Traction-Lok differential from the factory. On the outside, the GT500KR's 15-inch alloy wheels, which the seller says Shelby American refinished in 2005, sport Shelby center caps and feature BFGoodrich tires. Other exterior highlights include the grille-mounted Lucas fog lights, a rear spoiler, and a fiberglass hood with a working ram-air scoop.

The cabin is done in black knit-insert vinyl, covering both the front buckets and the Sport Deck rear seat. It also features the Interior Décor Group, which brings woodgrain accents to the dash, console, and doors, as well as the Visibility Group, which adds under-dash courtesy lamps along with lights for the glovebox, trunk, and engine bay.

A 2017 inspection report of the car by Kevin Marti highlights past rust repair and some Bondo. Notably, the battery-tray fender apron isn't original. According to the description, the car's engine and transmission were resealed in 2016, and in June of 2017, California emissions equipment was added. The seller mentions that the fuel cap, antenna, and fuel door were replaced recently, as were the starter and starter solenoid. While the selling dealer is a BaT Local Partner from Florida, the car has an Arkansas title.

There are 11 bids on this GT500 so far. But the current bid price seems quite low, at least for now, given that Hagerty's Price Guide puts a '68 GT500KR fastback in good condition between $117,000 and $140,000, and between $89,000 and $108,000 for a fair-condition car. The highest Hagerty reckons a concours-condition GT500KR fastback could be worth is around $235,000. What's interesting, however, is that this very GT500KR was previously sold for $201,000 on BaT in April 2022. And the car was featured again on the website in August 2026 but didn't quite meet the reserve, despite bids reaching as high as $240,000.

Whether this example will sell for its current bid price remains to be seen. Judging from its recent August appearance, though, that seems unlikely. If you fancy the car, go ahead and place your bid. The auction ends on Friday, November 27.

#5796. HLTH 2026: Viz.ai’s chief clinical officer on takeaways, goals of AI collab with National Rural Health Association

HLTH 2026: Viz.ai’s chief clinical officer on takeaways, goals of AI collab with National Rural Health Association" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

It’s been almost seven months since artificial intelligence disease detection and care coordination platform Viz.ai entered into a partnership with the National Rural Health Association (NRHA).

The partnership aims to help rural healthcare leaders better understand and implement AI tools across systems. That's been a personal and professional passion of Viz.ai Chief Clinical Officer Andrew Ibrahim, M.D., who discussed with Fierce Healthcare at HLTH his key takeaways from the collaboration thus far and forward-looking goals as it approaches its one-year mark.

Ibrahim said that the two organizations have done three educational events for rural health systems since the partnership kicked off in April. These series aim to show rural health administrators the specifics of AI—and whether they should adopt it, he said.

He noted there’s “sometimes a very big mismatch” when smaller rural health systems onboard multiple vendors.

“We've learned [that] many rural hospitals don't have the IT expertise and infrastructure to adopt some of these tools, and so it's actually been a force function to strengthen their hub spoke relationships,” Ibrahim said.

Strengthening these relationships, according to Ibrahim, has been key.

“It's actually been beautiful to see the hub-spoke relationship strengthened with the AI tool as the conduit,” Ibrahim said. “And it gives them a reason to interact more, and a way for the rural hospitals to strengthen their capabilities.”

He continued, “there's an authenticity about the moment where it's like ‘Yeah, we do need to help each other out.’ We're all kind of figuring it out as we go.”

In addition to the educational series, Ibrahim said frameworks are in development to aid rural health systems in navigating, implementing and deploying AI—which will be built into a toolkit.

One of Ibrahim’s personal goals for the one-year mark of the partnership is to ensure any rural health administrator can understand what an AI tool is when pitched.

“I think that would be a huge milestone,” he said. “Getting to 100% of hospitals at year one would be ideal—probably unrealistic, but that's probably the ultimate goal.”

And when it comes to metrics for measuring the collaboration, Ibrahim said he's looking for numbers that show participants are “keeping more care local” and retaining their workforces.

“It would be great to be able to connect the dots [and understand whether] adoption of an AI tool give[s] rural clinicians confidence, enthusiasm, willingness to stay in their community as opposed to dropping the services and moving back,” he said.

Another initiative from Viz that has “disproportionate benefit in rural communities,” according to Ibrahim, is its new partnership with Wolters Kluwer Health to integrate the Viz.ai One platform into UpToDate Expert AI.

“I'm pretty excited about being able to bring their level of clinical decision support into our rural hospitals,” he said.

#5795. How Can Energy Improve Lives? Why Counting Connections Isn’t Enough

Global tracking of energy access should expand beyond connections to include affordability, reliability, adequacy, and development outcomes.

Access to energy is a cornerstone of development—it can improve health, education, incomes, and overall quality of life.

But access is only the first step. A health clinic can’t perform surgery if frequent power cuts make its equipment unreliable. An electric irrigation pump is unlikely to raise a farmer’s income if crops can’t reach buyers. And a small business may gain little from electricity if it lacks financing to buy the equipment it needs to expand.

For energy to improve people’s lives, it must be affordable, sufficient, and reliable—and people and businesses must be able to put it to productive use.

The United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 7 (SDG 7) calls for “universal access to affordable, reliable, and modern energy services” by 2030. But the two indicators used to track its universal-access target focus only on whether people have access to electricity and whether they primarily rely on clean fuels and technologies. They do not address reliability, affordability, or economic impacts.

Other approaches already offer a fuller picture. The World Bank’s Energy Sector Management Assistance Program developed the Multi-Tier Framework to measure electricity access beyond connections, including whether electricity is available when needed, adequate for the equipment people want to use, reliable and affordable. While the framework is used by some countries to assess these broader dimensions of energy access, such measures are not the default, as many countries rely on the U.N.’s official global indicators.

As governments consider what should follow the SDGs after 2030, they should make multidimensional energy-access measures a regular part of national surveys and use the results to track progress globally. Since access alone does not necessarily deliver better livelihoods, improved measures of access could also be paired with indicators of whether energy is delivering the development outcomes it is intended to support. These could include whether clinics and schools can function as intended, farmers can increase yields and incomes and businesses can grow revenues and employment.

Together, these measures could shift energy planning from the largely supply-side question of how many people have access toward the demand-side questions of what people and institutions need energy for and whether the energy system enables them to meet these needs.

The examples below show why looking beyond connections matters in practice.

National electrification rates can mask large differences in where electricity is available within a country. Addressing those gaps requires looking beyond national averages to identify the households, businesses, and public facilities that lack access.

In 2023, WRI, working closely with Uganda’s Ministry of Health, used WRI’s Energy Access Explorer (EAE)—an online mapping tool that combines energy data with information on infrastructure, public services, and economic activity—to assess the electricity needs of health facilities. The analysis found that 675 facilities serving more than 3 million people had no electricity, either grid or off-grid, yet all were in areas with significant solar energy potential. The analysis helped identify places where solar power could fill the energy gap.

In Ethiopia, the Ministry of Water and Energy and the World Bank used EAE to help design a financing program for off-grid electricity. The analysis identified 145 priority woredas, or districts, where investments could reach more than 19 million people. Having this location-based data helped translate national energy-access goals into decisions about where public financing should be directed.

Ethiopia also illustrates why simple access figures can overstate the level of service people receive. A 2025 national energy-access survey found that 65% of households had access to at least one source of electricity. However, just 44% of the population received at least a basic level of electricity service, enough for uses such as lighting and charging a phone for at least four hours a day.

Simply having an electricity connection is not enough if the supply lacks the capacity or voltage stability to operate the equipment people need.

In the Gumla district in Jharkhand, India, villages that had gained household grid connections still lacked enough power for many businesses to function. WRI found that the single-phase electricity supplied was insufficient for productive uses such as milling and oil pressing. Beginning in 2015, Mlinda Charitable Trust, a nonprofit, installed solar mini-grids that supplied three-phase electricity, allowing local enterprises to run equipment, including rice and wheat hullers, oil expellers, flour mills, and pulverizers.

Governments should assess not only whether communities are connected but also whether the electricity supplied can meet the capacity and power-quality requirements of the services and equipment people need—and plan grid upgrades or complementary systems accordingly.

A connection provides limited benefit if households, businesses, or public facilities cannot pay for enough energy to meet their needs. Measuring meaningful access therefore also means asking whether the energy is affordable for the people and institutions expected to use it.

In Ethiopia’s Berbere district, farmers initially used petrol-powered pumps to irrigate their fields, but high fuel and maintenance costs meant these were too expensive for many to keep using. Petrol cost $91 to $203 per hectare a year, while repairs and the cost of transporting fuel added further expenses.

WRI and the Danish nonprofit DanChurchAid later installed two solar-powered pumps serving 48 farming households. The solar systems have no fuel costs, while maintenance costs are less than $10 a year, compared with more than $1,300 for petrol pumps. But the two pumps’ combined $19,200 upfront cost was beyond what most farmers could afford out of pocket. Governments and funders should therefore assess both the ongoing cost of using energy and the upfront cost of the technologies needed to use it, and provide financing or targeted support where high initial costs remain a barrier.

Being connected to the grid does not mean electricity will be available whenever it is needed. WRI researchers documented power cuts lasting three to 12 hours a day at two health facilities in Jharkhand, with outages worsening during the monsoon season. The facilities relied on diesel generators and small battery backups during outages.

In 2017, after solar photovoltaic systems and larger batteries were installed, the facilities were able to keep wards and offices running and power other essential equipment during grid outages, reducing their reliance on grid electricity.

Tracking the frequency and duration of outages would give a clearer picture of whether electricity is dependable enough to support essential services.

Even when energy is available, adequate, affordable, and reliable, it may not translate into better livelihoods. People also need equipment, financing, and access to markets to put energy to productive use.

In Uganda, WRI Africa and partners used EAE to identify $15 million in potential investments in renewable energy technologies, including solar-powered irrigation systems and equipment for cooling and milling, that could benefit more than 28,000 farmers. Some organizations identified through that work have since secured funding for related projects. Masaka District Farmers Association, for example, received an IKI Small Grants award for an irrigation project that equipped 150 hectares of coffee-growing land with drip irrigation and worked with 1,500 smallholder farmers.

In Berbere, solar-powered irrigation has enabled farmers to harvest three to four times a year and grow higher-value crops. In their first season, many farmers earned four to 10 times as much from onion, pepper, and cabbage sales as they had previously earned in a year from staple crops.

Tracking these outcomes alongside measures of energy access can help show whether investments are translating into higher productivity and incomes.

Making greater use of existing multidimensional measures, alongside complementary indicators of development outcomes, could change not just how governments report progress but also how they plan and direct investment.

Rather than starting with how many new connections a project can deliver, governments and funders would ask what people and institutions need energy for, what prevents them from using it effectively, and which investments could remove those barriers. In some places, that may mean extending electricity supply. In others, it could mean improving reliability, lowering costs, or helping farmers and businesses obtain the equipment and financing needed to use energy productively.

Energy is essential to improving human well-being, but it is only one part of what drives development. Like water, health care or education and energy is necessary but not sufficient. Treating access as a starting point rather than an end goal—and measuring whether people can use, afford, and rely on the energy they receive—would give governments a clearer picture of whether energy investments are improving people’s lives.

Courtesy of WRI. Experts: Dimitris Mentis, Harsha Meenawat

WRI is a global research organization that spans more than 50 countries, with offices in Brazil, China, Europe, India, Indonesia, and the United States. Our more than 450 experts and staff work closely with leaders to turn big ideas into action to sustain our natural resources—the foundation of economic opportunity and human well-being. Find out more at www.wri.org

#5793. New ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept: This Electric GTI Is Ready For The Racetrack

270 kW (367 PS), top speed of 240 km/h and 4.7 seconds from 0 to 100 km/h: With the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, Volkswagen is marking the 50th anniversary of the GTI by showing how uncompromising an electric GTI with motorsport ambitions can be. The concept car will be presented to the public next week at the Essen Motor Show (27 November to 6 December 2026). Its performance figures meet a two-door silhouette and flared wings as well as a large front splitter, diffuser and rear wing. The result: a powerful appearance and maximum downforce for fast laps. At the same time, the concept vehicle provides a preview of how the GTI idea can be further developed in the electric age.

Kai Grünitz, Member of the Board of Management for Technical Development, Volkswagen Brand and Brand Group Core: “The GTI has been one of Volkswagen’s great success stories for 50 years. This year, we launched our GTI as an electric vehicle in series production for the first time. With the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, we are showing how much more potential there is in the electric GTI world. Our platform strategy and MEB+ give us the technological freedom to make even extreme concepts possible.”

Designed for performance. The design of the new ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is based on the production model, the 166 kW (226 PS) ID. Polo GTI. In both models, the drive power is transmitted to the front axle. In the 270 kW (367 PS) ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept, this power delivery is controlled – thanks in part to an electronically regulated front differential lock (VAQ) – so that the model reaches 100 km/h from a standstill in just 4.7 seconds with Launch Control. Like the drive system, the electrical infrastructure has also been adapted to the high performance of the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept. The 52 kWh high-voltage battery can provide up to 290 kW at short notice, enabling a top speed of 240 km/h. The DCC (adaptive chassis control) has also been tuned for use on the racetrack and ensures precise handling and high traction in conjunction with the front differential lock. The new ceramic brakes of the one-box brake system are also designed for high performance.

Dynamics are visible in the design. On the exterior, the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept follows the powerful clarity of the ID. Polo GTI production model, while at the same time incorporating design elements that underline the motorsport characteristics. Particularly striking features are the two-door instead of four-door silhouette, pronounced flaring of the wings by 50 millimetres in each case, a large motorsport splitter at the front, a wider rear end, a new diffuser and a rear wing in carbon fibre that protrudes above the roof line.

Two-seater. Reduced to racing. The interior is also tailored to the racetrack, and only the basic layout of the overall cockpit has been adopted from the production model. This means there is no infotainment system, for example. The focus is solely on ergonomics and driving. The driver and front passenger sit on Recaro racing bucket seats with red 5-point harnesses. The rear and luggage compartment have been completely cleared. Instead of a rear seat system, a rollover bar painted in the GTI colour Tornado Red is integrated above and behind the front seats. The dash panel, side trims and many other details are covered in dark ArtVelours microfibre fabric with red topstitching – work that has been carried out with great precision by Volkswagen trainees. In many areas – in keeping with Volkswagen tradition – the young employees were directly involved in realisation of the concept vehicle by the Development department and designers.

550 instead of 290 newton-metres. The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept features the high-torque APP550 motor. The special technical challenge here: this motor is actually intended for the rear of large models such as the ID. Tiguan or ID.7. It therefore had to be fitted into the smaller ID. Polo as front-wheel drive and additionally combined with an electronic front differential lock. Thomas Schmall, Member of the Board of Management Volkswagen AG for Technology, and CEO of Volkswagen Group Components: “The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept shows just how emotive electric mobility can be: This is made possible by our APP550, one of the most efficient electric drives in its class. Manufactured over one million times at the Group Components plant in Kassel, this drive was actually developed for larger vehicle classes. Integrating it into the Polo required millimetre precision and is a powerful example of engineering skill and teamwork at Volkswagen, from Development and Design through to our trainees who worked on the project.”

GTI from the master of modular platforms. The ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is based on the modular electric drive (MEB+) platform with front-wheel drive. Volkswagen has used the basic technical layout of the production model and taken it to a new level of performance with a 104 kW (141 PS) more powerful electric drive. The result is the most dynamic interpretation of a front-wheel drive ID. model to date. At the other end of the scale is the Mission Efficiency, which is also based on the ID. Polo and set four world records as a particularly efficient near-production electric vehicle. Both concept vehicles show the large bandwidth offered by electric drive systems from maximum sportiness to outstanding efficiency.

2026 is the year of the GTI. Following the Golf GTI EDITION 50, the new ID.3 GTI (sales start early 2027) and the new ID. Polo GTI (available to order since October), the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport Concept is making its debut this year as the fourth new model under the umbrella of the iconic GTI product brand. No other compact sports car family has been as successful worldwide for half a century now – with more than 2.5 million units sold – as the GTI models.

#5792. Stellantis Is Pulling Out Of Every Racing Series It Competes In Except NASCAR

Stellantis is about to throw in the towel on just about every single one of its motorsports endeavors other than NASCAR... which it just re-entered after a 14-year hiatus. On November 23, it's expected that the automaker will convene two extraordinary works council meetings with the ultimate outcome being a withdrawal. That means Peugeot would leave endurance racing (which admittedly hasn't been going too well), Citroën and Opel would drop out of Formula E, and Lancia's reborn rally team would bite the dust.

The moves come as the automaker cuts costs across the board at the behest of CEO Antonio Filosa, according to Reuters. He's doing what he can to turn the company around after years of falling sales and weakening profitability. Earlier this year, Filosa launched a broad efficiency drive, known as the "Value Creation Program," and it targets about $6.6 billion in cost savings by 2028. Autocar reports that Stellantis Motorsport costs about $330 million a year to run, and cutting it could help with Stellantis' finances in Europe, where it just lost $341 million in the third quarter alone.

This isn't the first time something like this has happened for Peugeot. Its former owners, PSA, quit the 24 Hours of Le Mans back in 2012 in an effort to save cash, and it didn't rejoin until 2022.

It is, nevertheless, still strange timing. As I mentioned, Dodge just re-entered NASCAR. On top of that, French outlet L'Automobile reports that Peugeot has a redesigned 9x8 for its 2027 WEC endurance program and Citroën and Opel have been working on their new Gen4 car for Formula E with new technical partners. It's likely that the team that runs Citroën, MSG Racing, will continue with a new sponsor.

Hell, Open is technically making its debut in FE this upcoming season. It was just announced in March of this year when the brand signed a four-year contract to compete with the new Gen4 cars.

Lancia's WRC re-entry is another sacrificial lamb at the altar of financial prudence. The Lancia Corse HF team started in the WRC2 category this year, Autocar reports. It entered its gas-powered Ypsilon Rally2 HF Integrale, and it has even racked up a few wins. More likely than not, customer teams will continue to be supported, though.

Motorsports are usually what's first to get cut when an automaker is struggling. Earlier this year, Alpine dropped out of WEC, citing a tough market, and Porsche did the same thing back in 2025.

#5791. Department of Labor moves to end expedited green cards for nurses, physical therapists

Department of Labor moves to end expedited green cards for nurses, physical therapists" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The U.S. Department of Labor proposed new policy this week that would end fast-track green cards for healthcare professionals like nurses and physical therapists—the latest in a string of policies from the Trump administration raising the bar for foreign-born workers and students across healthcare and other industries.

Currently, nurses, physical therapists and other workers “with exceptional ability in the sciences or arts” are granted an exemption from an administrative test in the permanent labor certification program (PERM), a months-long administrative process in which an employer must prove there are no able, willing, qualified and available U.S. workers for a permanent job ahead of sponsoring a foreign worker.

The exemption, referred to Schedule A, is given to occupations where the DOL recognizes a nationwide shortage of U.S. workers. Nurses and physical therapists have been listed under Schedule A for more than 30 years.

The Department of Labor, in its newly proposed rule, said it wants to eliminate Schedule A as it cannot “demonstrate that the occupations currently listed in Schedule A are still shortage occupations.”

It cited in the proposed rule a late 2023 request for information published under the Biden administration seeking input on potentially expanding Schedule A. Despite more than 2,000 responses, DOL now says it didn’t receive the information it would need to establish a methodology for regularly reviewing and updating Schedule A occupations, and questioned whether it has the statutory authority to make such occupational exemptions in the first place.

“The elimination of Schedule A would enable the Department to better ensure that U.S. workers have an opportunity to apply for available job opportunities, and adhere to the statutory requirements to protect U.S. workers assigned to it, as intended by Congress under the [Immigration and Nationality Act].”

The proposed rule, which is open to public comment for 60 days, also includes requirements for employers to advertise their open jobs more broadly and for a longer period of time to demonstrate a good-faith effort to recruit American workers before turning to a green card sponsorship. These and other proposed changes would be the first “comprehensive” reforms to the PERM program in almost two decades, the Department of Labor said.

If finalized as-is, employers who want to sponsor professional nurses, physical therapists and other affected roles “would be required to go through the lengthier and costlier PERM labor market testing process, adding time, cost and administrative work to a pathway that hospitals, nursing homes and rehabilitation providers have historically relied on to fill persistent shortages,” Caroline Tang, an Austin shareholder at labor and employment law firm Ogletree Deakins, told Fierce Healthcare.

Industry associations as well as other sections of the government have widely projected shortages in the healthcare workforce, including nurses, for the coming years. The Heart Resources and Services Association’s National Center for Health Workforce Analysis, for instance, projects (PDF) national shortages of registered nurses through at least 2038, with a projected 8% shortage in 2028 that is more severe in non-metro areas.

The proposed policy change is among several brought by the Trump administration in line with an order from the White House to prioritize domestic hiring—though many have been stymied in the courts.

Among the most prominent is a $100,000 supplemental fee the Department of Homeland Security attached to H-1B petitions that was vacated by two separate judged, and in August was succeeded by the somewhat altered proposal of an additional H-1B petition fee of $103,265. Another policy from the same department tightening how long nonimmigrant students may remain in the country (referred to as “duration of status”) was temporary blocked hours before implementation in September and fully vacated on Monday (PDF), though the former decision is already being appealed.

The Department of Labor has also proposed increasing the prevailing wage floors for several green cards that legal experts expect will be challenged by employers that would shoulder the resulting financial burden.

#5790. Alzheimer's Light and Sound Stimulation Therapy Misses Main Goal in Pivotal Trial

— But gamma wave approach hints at slower decline in mild Alzheimer's disease

A novel Alzheimer's therapy platform that delivered 40 Hz light and sound stimulation to engage gamma-frequency brain activity did not meet its primary endpoint, the HOPE pivotal study showed.

In the primary analysis population of 663 people with mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's, the change from baseline on a composite measure of Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and Alzheimer's Disease Cooperative Study-Activities of Daily Living (ADCS-ADL) scores did not differ between those who used the Spectris stimulation goggles or sham at 12 months, reported Marwan Sabbagh, MD, of the Barrow Neurological Institute in Phoenix.

Secondary endpoints in the overall study population also showed no significant differences. However, a prespecified subgroup analysis of 395 people with mild Alzheimer's disease (MMSE scores of 21-28 on the 30-point scale) showed favorable results for the device on some measures, Sabbagh said at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer's Disease conference in Boston.

In the mild subgroup, the device was associated with a 55.8% slowing of decline in ADCS-ADL scores (nominal P=0.016) and a 46.8% slowing of decline in Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB) scores (nominal P=0.004), Sabbagh noted.

Results in the moderate subgroup (MMSE scores of 15-20) did not favor the device, and some outcomes nominally favored sham.

The difference in outcomes between mild and moderate disease suggests that earlier intervention may be key to clinical benefit, observed Laura Nisenbaum, PhD, interim chief science officer at the Alzheimer's Drug Discovery Foundation in New York City, which provided funding for the trial.

"While the HOPE study did not meet its primary endpoint, the signal in the mild Alzheimer's subgroup raises important questions that are worth exploring further," Nisenbaum said. "Daily function is what patients and families tell us matters most, so it will be important to see whether the early signs of slower decline on that measure in people with mild Alzheimer's hold up as more data become available."

The device delivers audiovisual stimulation intended to evoke steady-state gamma oscillations across broad cortical regions, Sabbagh explained. "Spectris was developed as a non-invasive, home-use investigational medical device that delivers daily 1-hour treatment sessions," he said.

Earlier research showed that sensory-evoked 40 Hz neural activity engages brain mechanisms essential for cognition and daily function, he added.

The HOPE trial evaluated the device in participants who had baseline MMSE scores of 15-28 and Alzheimer's biomarker confirmation. Participants were randomized within stratified mild and moderate disease subgroups.

The primary outcome was the integrated Alzheimer's Disease MMSE and ADCS-ADL Rating Scale, an equally weighted composite of global cognition (MMSE) and daily function (ADCS-ADL) scores, Sabbagh said.

In the overall study population, adverse device effects were reported in 18.3% of participants who received active treatment and 15.5% who received sham. The most common were headache, tinnitus, fatigue, dizziness, and ear pain. Seizures occurred in 0.9% of the active treatment group.

The gamma wave approach to treating Alzheimer's disease was first discovered in 2014 at the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). Executives at Cognito Therapeutics, an MIT spin-off, said they will pursue FDA approval for the 40 Hz light and sound stimulation device based on the nominally significant benefits seen in the mild Alzheimer's population.

An open-label extension of the HOPE trial is ongoing.

#5789. Study raises doubts about combining vaccine, monoclonal antibody to protect against malaria

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Andrew covers the biopharma industry, scientific research, and public health across the continent. You can reach Andrew confidentially on Signal at drewqjoseph.71.

When it comes to preventing malaria, researchers and public health officials have been hopeful about the potential of a monoclonal antibody, one injection of which could provide recipients with several months of protection against the parasite. Such a tool, experts have thought, could give babies a layer of defense even before they start receiving doses of the malaria vaccines that have rolled out in recent years.

New research detailed Thursday has cast doubt on that strategy.

Scientists tested the monoclonal, known as L9LS, in infants in Mali, finding that it was 78% effective versus a placebo in providing protection against the malaria parasite over the six-month transmission season, similar to what has been seen in studies of the antibody in older kids and adults.

However, they also reported that it interfered with the immune response the malaria vaccine R21 elicits, resulting in a 20% to 30% drop in antibody levels generated by the immunization, according to an abstract presented at the annual meeting of the American Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene.

While it’s not clear what the diminished immune responses seen in blood tests would mean for the real-world protection offered by the vaccine, researchers say they’re going to focus on groups other than babies as they plan the pivotal studies that could lead to L9LS being approved, which they hope to start in 2028.

“We have these other clear use cases, so let’s get those done and get it approved and we can come back and revisit this,” said Robert Seder of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, whose lab helped develop L9LS.

There is no panacea against malaria, and various strategies come with advantages and disadvantages that public health officials have to weigh as they think about which approach to prioritize and for whom, particularly given the limited funding for a disease that predominantly affects poor countries. The infection killed about 610,000 people in 2024, the majority of them children under 5 years old in sub-Saharan Africa.

R21 and RTS,S, the two malaria vaccines, are seen as major scientific breakthroughs — they are the first vaccines against any parasite — but they require multiple doses to be effective, the first of which comes at 5 months of age. They do, however, provide some level of protection for years.

A monoclonal, on the other hand, can provide several months of protection with just one dose, which could be enough to cover recipients for peak transmission periods. (In areas with year-round transmission, deploying antibodies might require two to three doses a year, experts say.) It could offer an alternative to the current strategy of giving children existing antimalarial treatments every month during high-transmission periods, which is a cheap and effective preventive strategy but that opens the door to adherence challenges.

“A monoclonal antibody, with only one shot, provides an efficacy over six months, and those six months correspond to the season of malaria in Sahelian regions,” said Kassoum Kayentao of Mali’s University of Sciences, Techniques, and Technologies of Bamako, one of the experts involved with the new research. “In terms of logistics, in terms of programmatical use, this could be a very good tool.”

The constraint with antibodies is that they are comparatively costly, though there are efforts underway to bring down the price of each dose as researchers head to pivotal trials.

The new study enrolled infants from 1 month to 12 months, gave them either a placebo or the L9LS monoclonal, and then doses of the R21 vaccine. That sequence was what created the issue, researchers said.

The malaria vaccines work by training the immune system to recognize a protein on the parasite known as the circumsporozoite protein, or CSP. The monoclonal L9LS also binds to the CSP. That meant that, when the infants who had been given L9LS later received R21, the antibody bound to the vaccine as well, essentially interfering with the full immune response it was meant to trigger, researchers believe.

All the health and medical news you need today, in one email

Experts said there were still key groups of people who could benefit from a monoclonal and who could be the focus of future studies. Among them are pregnant people, as an infection during pregnancy can be dangerous for both parent and baby. Kids who are hospitalized with malaria are another target group. In the months after they’re released from hospital and as they recover from the infection-caused anemia, they are particularly vulnerable to severe outcomes from another malaria case. The current strategy of what’s called post-discharge malaria chemoprevention involves taking available preventive drugs every month, whereas one shot of a monoclonal as they leave the hospital could cover them for months.

André-Marie Tchouatieu of the Medicines for Malaria Venture, who was not involved in the study, said that, despite the issue seen with L9LS and the vaccine, it did not limit the potential impact the monoclonal and next-generation versions could have in reducing the burden of malaria broadly.

“Definitely there will be a use case,” said Tchouatieu, who this month co-authored a New England Journal of Medicine review outlining the advantages and challenges of different malaria strategies. “Every tool that can prove efficacy and safety will have a role to play in the whole strategy for malaria elimination.”

#5787. F1 Finally Hiring Permanent Race Stewards, Replacing Volunteer Officials

Unlike the typical ball sports, a significant number of on-track rule infractions are strictly tied to a specific penalty. The punishment is selected from a set range by part-time volunteers who are often criticized by drivers, teams and fans for their inconsistency. The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile announced on Thursday that it will be introducing full-time stewards to officiate Formula 1 next season. The sport's global governing body is finally shedding one of the last vestiges of its aristocratic past, aiming to provide more consistent rule calls. Welcome to 21st century, F1.

The transition to full-time professional officials likely won't be completed by the start of the 2027 season. The FIA stated it's establishing a department of 12 to 15 full-time stewards recruited from its existing pool of international stewards. While they will initially complement the current part-timers, the role of the permanent stewards will expand as their roster grows. Beyond officiating F1 race weekends, the full-timers will form a constant rule-decision base and train their eventual successors with those precedents. FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem said:

"This latest major investment in FIA officiating reflects our dedication to delivering the highest standards of decision-making, fairness and integrity in motorsport. The recruitment of full-time stewards is a significant step in our longstanding mission of building a dedicated officiating ecosystem in the FIA Formula One World Championship, it is also an investment in the future of our sport."

Formula 1 was formed in the same aristocratic primordial pool of international sports that encouraged the International Olympic Committee to ban professional athletes until 1986. European aristocrats held the reins of international motorsport until that same period. Prince Paul Alfons von Metternich-Winneburg finished a decade as FIA President in 1985. If the Metternich name sounds familiar, he was a great-grandson of Prince Klemens von Metternich, the influential 19th-century Austrian statesman.

While F1 has become a multi-billion-dollar enterprise, the championship's officiating has long remained locked in an era when amateurism was a virtue. As a result, the F1 stewards' office is filled with people who can afford to spend significant time and money earning the prerequisite credentials and gaining the necessary experience officiating smaller events. The unpaid volunteers are often successful lawyers and automotive executives, sometimes employed by companies directly involved in F1. Thankfully, those days are finally coming to an end.

#5786. Opinion: The U.S. lost measles elimination status. The next Congress should help restore it

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Kuppalli is an infectious diseases physician with experience in frontline outbreak response, preparedness, and policy for emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases. She writes ID Consult, a STAT column about infectious diseases.

On Tuesday, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) announced that the United States had lost its measles elimination status, a distinction it had held for 26 years. The same lineage of the virus has spread from person to person in the United States for at least a year, meeting the criteria for measles transmission to be considered reestablished. In communities where measles is still spreading, children have more chances to be exposed, including infants too young for their first routine vaccine dose. The risk of exposure also rises for people who are immunocompromised, such as transplant recipients who take medications that suppress their immune systems.

The deaths reported this November show how quickly a decade of progress can unravel. New York reported that a child in Lewis county had died, the state’s first known measles-associated death in more than 30 years. Wisconsin reported its first measles death since 1990, an infant, and announced the death of a second child eight days later. In Pennsylvania, two deaths reported earlier in November brought the state’s tally to seven for the year. A day after PAHO announced that the United States had lost its measles elimination status, Pennsylvania confirmed its eighth measles-associated death this year, an unvaccinated resident of Clinton county.

When the current administration took office in January 2025, the United States had gone nearly a decade without a reported measles death. A month later, in February 2025, an unvaccinated child died in the West Texas outbreak.

As cases mounted last year, my colleague and I wrote in The Lancet that the Texas outbreak showed how quickly gaps in vaccination coverage could jeopardize the country’s measles elimination status. We called for sustained investment in routine immunization with targeted vaccination campaigns, strengthening public health communication and community engagement to build vaccine confidence, and resources for health departments to detect cases and contain outbreaks before they spread.

As of Nov. 13, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had recorded more than 5,400 cases, more than twice the total for all of 2025. This number reflects confirmed cases reported to the CDC and is likely an undercount.

Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, and New York have reported a total of 11 measles-associated deaths this year. The CDC’s provisional national count is six. The agency now relies on national death certificate data, which can take time to process. State health departments can identify deaths through outbreak investigations and may use different criteria to determine whether measles contributed.

The federal death count could rise as more records come in and reviews are completed. While the CDC works with state epidemiologists on a common definition, it should explain publicly why the counts differ.

To regain elimination status, the United States must interrupt sustained transmission for at least 12 months and show, through reliable surveillance, that it has done so. That work starts in the schools and neighborhoods where children are missing doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. Two doses of the MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles. Yet vaccination coverage among U.S. kindergartners fell from 95.2% in the 2019–20 school year to 92.4% in 2025–26, leaving an estimated 280,000 kindergarteners without the protection of both doses. Even in states with high overall coverage, measles can spread quickly in schools and communities where there are pockets of unvaccinated people.

In its first funding bills, the new Congress should protect the Vaccines for Children program and provide multiyear funding for health departments to work with schools and pediatric practices in communities with the lowest vaccination coverage. It should pay for staff who can call families whose children are overdue, answer questions about vaccine side effects, help them find immunization records, and offer appointments after school or on Saturdays. By Nov. 13, Pennsylvania’s state health center staff had administered more than 7,100 MMR doses at pop-up clinics in affected communities. Health departments should be able to do that work before an outbreak. Congress can track whether the funding is reaching those communities by asking where coverage is improving, down to the county or school district where data allow.

Some parents want to talk through their questions before making a vaccination appointment. When I helped lead Covid-19 vaccination efforts in South Carolina, and still in my practice today, I hear those questions firsthand. People want to know what the evidence shows, what we are still learning, what side effects to expect, and which recommendations have changed over time and why. They want enough information to make an empowered decision for themselves and their families.

To help them do that, health workers and public health officials need reliable access to the scientific evidence behind vaccine recommendations and time to sit down with patients and meaningfully talk through their questions.

In a nationally representative survey of U.S. adults that my colleagues and I presented at IDWeek 2026, more than half expressed confidence in the accuracy of the CDC’s vaccine information. When we asked whom they would trust if sources disagreed, 30% chose the CDC. Respondents put the most trust in their own health care providers. That trust matters because a clinician who knows a patient’s medical history can explain what the evidence means for that person and address the questions that may shape their decision.

The incoming House and Senate health committees should hold public hearings where Department of Health and Human Services leaders are asked to explain the evidence behind changes to vaccine recommendations made over the past two years. What evidence did they review? Whom did they consult? If they departed from their scientific advisers’ recommendations, why? Congress should require HHS to publish those answers when it announces a change. A pediatrician talking with a parent that afternoon should be able to explain the decision.

The same health departments that help schools close vaccination gaps also have to respond when a clinician calls about a suspected case. They need someone to answer after hours, a lab that can test a specimen promptly, and staff who can reach exposed families while there’s still time to help. Congress should fund that capacity year-round and direct HHS and the CDC to publish a plan for regaining elimination status, with clear responsibilities and deadlines.

Congress should also ask the CDC to report publicly each quarter on whether two-dose MMR coverage is rising in the communities with the largest gaps and if it is not increasing, to explain what the challenges are to vaccination. The agency should also provide information about how quickly suspect cases are investigated and where chains of transmission remain active.

These reports would help Congress understand where more help is needed and build the record the U.S. needs to demonstrate at least 12 months without sustained measles transmission.

I’ve spent much of my career responding to outbreaks after opportunities to prevent them had passed. In early 2025 when the measles outbreak emerged in Texas, I was worried that we were on the path to lose elimination status. Now I am reading reports of deaths in states that haven’t had one in decades. The next Congress should start with a hearing that puts HHS on the record about how it will regain elimination status. It should also make sure that its first funding bill allocates resources to ensure communities can vaccinate children and those at risk to stop outbreaks. Every month we wait leaves more families exposed to a deadly disease we know how to prevent.

Krutika Kuppalli, M.D., is an infectious diseases physician with experience in frontline outbreak response, preparedness, and policy for emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases. She writes STAT’s ID Consult column. The views expressed here are her own and do not necessarily reflect those of any organization she is affiliated with.

#5785. UnitedHealthcare's new care model leans on community pharmacies

UnitedHealthcare's new care model leans on community pharmacies" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealthcare is teaming up with CPSEN for a new program that will lean on community pharmacists to reach Medicaid patients.

The insurance giant said Wednesday that its through the UHC Pharmacy Care Hub model, pharmacists will work alongside the payer's care managers and providers to help close gaps in care and support management for chronic conditions and other needs.

Participating pharmacies will offer a range of services, including telehealth, medication management, point-of-care testing and personalized supports. The program is built on a hub-and-spoke model, where pharmacists can then help lead the patient to the right site of care or through any follow-up if needed.

These interactions can also help track patterns in emergency care use, and help patients find a more appropriate setting if their needs aren't emergent.

The program is currently available to UnitedHealthcare Medicaid members in seven states: Florida, Kansas, Michigan, Missouri, North Carolina, Tennessee and Virginia. UHC expects to add additional states throughout the year.

Part of the goal, the company said, is to tap into the trust that local pharmacists have in the communities they serve.

“Community pharmacies are trusted, local access points for care,” said Arethusa Kirk, M.D., chief medical officer for UnitedHealthcare Community & State, in the announcement. “This new model expands the services independent pharmacists can help deliver, making it easier for people—especially those facing barriers to care—to get timely support closer to home.”

UHC said that most (89%) of Americans live within five miles of a pharmacy, making these locations an easier option to access for many. This is especially true for individuals who may struggle to find an appointment with a doctor or find transportation to a visit.

For example, a participating pharmacist in North Carolina, Madeline Clark, said in the announcement that a patient came into the pharmacy for a urine test, as she had a potential urinary tract infection. The pharmacy conducted the test and sent the results virtually to a provider through UnitedHealthcare's Doctor Chat tool.

A prescription was then filled for the patient in the same visit, and she was out the door within about 30 minutes.

Clark said the patient was thankful not just for the ease of that trip to the pharmacy but for avoiding a visit to the ER as well.

"Not only was this a lower cost of care in the healthcare system space, but it also was just incredibly helpful for the patient," she said.

#5784. JA Energy Storage Launches an Internal Battery Passport Platform to Facilitate Compliance with EU Standards

JJA ESS has launched its own battery passport data platform to support lifecycle information management and help companies prepare for upcoming EU regulations. The platform is hosted in the company’s own cloud environment, giving the team direct responsibility for data policies, access permissions, and future updates.

According to the EU Battery Regulation, from February 18, 2027, battery passports are mandatory for batteries used in light vehicles (LMTs), electric vehicles, and industrial batteries with a capacity exceeding 2 kWh that are placed on the market or put into service. Further requirements will follow.

A battery passport is a digital data record linked to a single physical battery. A QR code and a unique identifier based on the ISO/IEC 15459 series connect the data record to the battery, enabling access to information throughout its entire lifecycle. This can include product identity, material composition, CO₂ footprint, recycled content, performance and durability, condition, supply chain due diligence, and end-of-life disposal. Taken together, these data points support consistent information management from product identification to the end of the product lifecycle.

For manufacturers, the challenge lies not simply in creating a QR code. The data must be traceable back to its source, up-to-date, and accessible in accordance with regulatory and business requirements. Companies must also manage access to sensitive information and comply with regulations governing cross-border data transfers and trade secrets. This balance is particularly relevant for companies operating in multiple markets. When companies utilize a third-party platform, its functionality, access to data fields, and interoperability can be determined by the provider’s configuration and service model.

JA ESS developed the platform internally and hosts it in its own cloud environment. Data policies, access permissions, and future platform updates are managed by the JA ESS internal team. This team ensures compliance with EU regulations regarding data access, presentation, and updates, while also giving JA ESS greater control over data management. The platform can also evolve as regulatory requirements change and real-world applications provide further insights.

JA ESS is the energy storage business unit under the JA brand. As a central component of JA’s energy storage strategy, JA ESS offers a wide range of FTM and BTM applications with safe, efficient, intelligent, and customized solutions for the large-scale, commercial, and industrial sectors as well as the residential market.

#5783. The Benz-Branded Mercedes SL Is Coming Back

When Mercedes introduced the seventh-generation R232 SL roadster, it was only offered in performance-oriented AMG trims, with an ultra-luxury Maybach variant coming a few years later. For the first time in the model's history, a Benz-branded SL was missing from the lineup, but that's about to change because of buyer feedback. Some folks apparently miss the subdued, grand touring nature that SLs of old provided, and they don't all have the $230,000 it takes to enter Maybach land, so a Mercedes-Benz SL is coming back.

With this current generation, Mercedes wanted to bring the SL and AMG GT Coupe closer together, and it seems that may have been a slight miscalculation on the German automaker's part. While big power and big prices are all well and good, it's not exactly what the average SL owner is looking for — especially when the Mercedes-AMG GT Coupe exists, according to Autocar. They missed some of the refinement and long-distance cruising ability of the old cars. Basically, the new one was hurting their agining backs.

Now that its mid-cycle refresh time, the GT will remain the performance-oriented vehicle, and the SL will take on a more relaxed demeaner, CEO Ola Källenius told Autocar. It'll trade in rock hard suspension and track times for comfort and ride quality. The two vehicles will also get revised engines to meet new emissions standards in Communist Europe.

Mercedes will discontinue the entry-level SL43 and GT43 that use a turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-4, and the same fate will befall the SL63 S E Performance and its 805-horsepower plug-in-hybrid V8 powertrain. Instead, the updated SLs will all get 48-volt mild-hybrid systems, and the new entry-level engine is expected to be a 443-hp turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-6, which is far more befitting of a grand tourer anyway. That model will probably be called SL500, while an SL580 will have the new M177 Evo flat-plane crank V8 we first saw in the refreshed S-Class.

Don't worry, drop-top AMG fans. The AMG SL isn't going anywhere, even if the E Performance is. Autocar speculates that the M177 will be also used in an SL63 that'll put out a notch over 600 horsepower, which should be more than enough for the folks who are into things of that nature. (The AMG SL55 will effectively be replaced by the V8 Benz SL580.)

It's not just an ethos change, either. Mercedes says the Benz SL will have front-end styling that alighes closer with the standard Mercedes look, with a simpler grille that has one horizontal bar across it rather than the more aggressive AMG grille with all its vertical canes. It'll also make use of the latest Digital Light headlight system from the company, which, of course, features three-pointed-star daytime running lights. Inside, the car will get an upgraded MB.OS platform to run the infotainment and the rest of the car's brain as well as some new physical control.

If this all sounds exciting to you in a way that the AMG SL didn't, well, you've got to hold on just a little bit longer. Källenius says the refreshed SL, which is going to be "more of a Mercedes-Benz," is expected to lauch in 2027.

#5781. Novel Oral HAE Drug Measures Up to Injectable Options

— Randomized trial hits the mark for reducing hereditary angioedema attack rates

Prophylactic use of the novel oral bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist deucrictibant substantially reduced hereditary angioedema (HAE) attacks, a pivotal phase III trial showed.

For the primary endpoint, extended-release deucrictibant lowered the attack rate by a relative 83%, to 0.35 events per month compared with 2.06 in the placebo group (P<0.0001), reported Marc A. Riedl, MD, of the University of California San Diego, at the American College of Allergy, Asthma & Immunology annual meeting.

During the 24-week treatment period in the CHAPTER-3 trial, 45% of study drug-treated patients were attack free, compared with 3% of the placebo group (P=0.0018).

"We don't have head-to-head studies, but it is in the same ballpark of what the subcutaneous long-term prophylactic drugs have shown," Riedl told MedPage Today. "This is what we were hoping to see as investigators -- this high level of efficacy in a once-daily pill."

That's meaningful given what's been seen with the only approved targeted oral HAE prophylactic medication, berotralstat (Orladeyo), Riedl noted.

"The overall efficacy, at least in the pivotal trial for berotralstat, didn't measure up quite as well compared to some of the subcutaneous treatment options for long-term prophylaxis," he said. "So this is an effort to try to look at another oral agent that might be more effective across the population, just given that we know some patients really prefer oral medication for convenience and less burden of treatment and so forth."

Of the 85 patients in the trial, five had genetically confirmed HAE with normal C1 inhibitor levels. While two of three of these patients on deucrictibant had good results with the drug -- one had a greater than 80% reduction and the other had 100% reduction in HAE attacks -- the third patient had only a very small reduction in attack rate.

A post-hoc analysis looking at only patients with deficiency or dysfunction of C1 inhibitor levels showed an 87% reduction in attack rate with deucrictibant, a rate that Riedl said "reflects the type 1 and type 2 HAE population that every other study has reported when they report out their efficacy data for prophylaxis."

The international trial enrolled patients ages 12 years and older (mean age 39) who had at least three attacks within 3 months before screening and at least two attacks during the up to 8-week run-in period. Participants were randomly assigned 2:1 to 24 weeks of double-blind treatment with extended-release deucrictibant (40 mg once a day) or placebo.

Baseline HAE attack rate was 3.8 per month in the study drug group and 3.5 per month in the placebo group. Attack rates dropped within the first week with deucrictibant and remained lower than in the placebo group through week 24.

The relative reductions in events that required rescue medication and in moderate-to-severe HAE attacks were 83% and 77%, respectively (both P<0.0001). Nearly all patients on deucrictibant had their attack rate reduced by at least 70% (96% vs 23% on placebo, P<0.0001). The drug increased the proportion of patients who had at least a 90% reduction in attack frequency as well (65% vs 10%, P<0.0001). Deucrictibant also resulted in significantly greater improvements in mean Angioedema Quality of Life questionnaire total score and all domain scores as compared with placebo.

Riedl called the safety profile favorable overall. One treatment-emergent serious adverse event occurred in the deucrictibant group, a case of laryngeal dyskinesia that resulted in a stay in the intensive care unit for evaluation but was deemed not related to the study drug.

The sole discontinuation in the active treatment group was due to asymptomatic elevation in liver function tests. Riedl noted that this is in line with what has been seen in most of the long-term prophylactic studies with HAE medications. "These patients do sometimes have a history of fatty liver. They've been on androgens, which we know can affect their liver function," he said.

Gastrointestinal side effects seen with berotralstat were not observed with deucrictibant (1.8% vs 6.7% on placebo).

An immediate-release version of deucrictibant is also being developed for on-demand treatment of acute HAE attacks and is under review by the FDA for that indication. Riedl suggested that if the extended-release formulation were to be approved as an additional prophylactic treatment option, it could be appealing for patients who prefer oral medications over injections.

"This would potentially be an oral treatment that gives very similar efficacy in terms of preventing attacks compared to what we've seen with the subcutaneous drugs, and we don't actually have that at the moment," he said.

He pointed to the increasing options for HAE management as good for patients. "Trying to make that preventative treatment as easy, as least burdensome as we can is part of the goal," Riedl noted. "And I think this is one way to potentially do that for people -- just a once-daily medication that's portable, easy to travel with, and makes their lives easier."

In its announcement, Aetna notes that data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention show that about 90% of pregnancy-related deaths could have been prevented, with a lack of access to prenatal care and more complete support making for a key barrier.

"This is a national access issue, a quality issue, and it's an affordability problem," she said.

In addition, it's not uncommon for programs that aim to drive better maternal outcomes to lack services for the babies, who in the first year of life undergo a wide array of critical developmental milestones, Guerraz said.

Aetna, as the third-largest insurer in the U.S., sees about 200,000 deliveries a year among its members. That means the success of this program could have a significant impact in a short amount of time, supporting at least 1 million babies over the next five years, she said.

Aetna for You and Baby also builds on a broader push within the company to build a more personalized and simple experience for members. For instance, the company established a program that embeds Aetna nurses in the hospital to support discharge planning and transitions for members, and Guerraz said that holds potential in the maternal care space.

For example, if a baby needs to stay in the neonatal intensive care unit after birth, having an Aetna nurse in the NICU providing additional support to the clinical team and the member would pay dividends, she said.

Aetna is also plugged into Health 100, a sister subsidiary of its parent company, CVS Health, that offers an AI-powered tool to help patients identify healthcare costs and navigate their benefits, even if they're not members of Aetna or Caremark or CVS Pharmacy customers.

Guerraz said the program is designed to offer something that patients can carry with them if their coverage changes.

She added that the team intends to continue iterating on the program and identifying other barriers to care for moms and their babies.

"This is something that we know is going to have a massive impact," she said.

#5778. Scion FR-S, Mercedes-Benz 240D, Suzuki Sidekick: The Dopest Cars I Found For Under $5,000

Friends, I'm going to give you a little peek behind the curtain at how this, your most beloved weekly automotive column, works. It goes like this: I find a bunch of car listings, and then I write a couple thousand words about them. You might expect the former to be the fun part, browsing all week for new and interesting listings, but it's actually the back half I really enjoy. See, finding listings has a problem: Eventually, things get old.

That's why you need gimmicks. Cars from a certain area, cars with a certain theme, cars from history's greatest cinematic achievement. Today, the gimmick is price: A hard cap of $5,000, which no vehicle exceeds. I honestly expected a bunch of beige commuter cars in questionable stated of repair, but I'm shocked at how good the offerings were in rust-free states. We've got Benzes, BMWs, and bikes as far as the eye can see. Welcome, my friends, to a budget-conscious edition of the week's Dopest Cars.

Remember when nice FR-Ses or BRZs cost five figures? Well, they still do. This example is no one's definition of immaculate, but it should be everyone's definition of a deal. This is Miata money! Less than Miata money! For under five grand, you could have one of the best-handling chassis out there, and with an engine that's not even blown! Yet. Probably.

Even if/when that does happen, $5,000 leaves plenty of room in the budget for something new to go under that theoretically carbon hood. K-swap, 2JZ, RB26, LS, EJ257, everything fits. Do whatever you want forever with this car, because it's up for whatever. You can fit anything between those front wheels, and you should. Do something cool with it, then reach out to me and send me pictures and videos of the cool thing you did. I'll write about it. That's an Amber promise. (Amber does not get to make these promises. -Ed)

Not only is there a new liquid-cooled replacement for this old 411cc Himalayan out there, in the form of the Himalayan 450, but there's now a bigger brother in Enfield's adventure lineup with the Himi 750. This is neither of those, but they're still relevant here because their very existence makes the first-generation Himalayan cheaper by comparison. It's slower, less powerful, and altogether not as advanced a bike — perfect for those of you looking to get started with something approachable.

Personally, I see the appeal in a dead-simply little ADV like the Himalayan 411. There's so little to go wrong, it's the kind of adventure bike that you can actually really adventure with. Sure, service intervals aren't Honda long, but good luck getting an Africa Twin for three grand. The Himalayan won't get you anywhere fast, it won't be the most stylish way around, but it'll certainly get you where you're going.

Yeah, I was surprised too. A Z32 300ZX, in seemingly good shape, for under $5,000. Are cars just free in the states where they don't rust away into dust after two winters? Do you Arizonans just have your pick of any cool car you want for approximately the price of a Costco hot dog? Don't tell me. I can't bear to know.

Anyway, this 300ZX isn't perfect, so at least I can take some solace in that while I scroll my locally-available rustbuckets and cry myself to sleep. It needs a whole wheel bearing, something that's surely a pain to replace on a completely rust-free car where none of the undercarriage bolts have fused to each other and become one piece of metal that's inseparable no matter how much heat and torque you apply. Surely that's the case. Please just let me have this one. Not even this car, just this dream of perfect-car availability outside my region.

Pink R6! Well, pinkish gray. It's pinker than any factory fairings for the bike, at least. Actually, none of you are allowed to buy this one, I want it for myself once I win a quick Powerball. Just keep scrolling to the next slide.

Mister Two? More like mister too expensive, except in Southern California where these can apparently be had for $4,500. I see why so many car and bike people live there, with the beautiful roads and temperate climate and availability of cars that aren't just piled of rust with a VIN. I get the appeal, but unfortunately I can never join you all. If I spend more than five days in LA I start to go mad due to lack of walkable infrastructure.

Anyway, MR2. This one's not a turbo car, but that doesn't really matter for this kind of money. It also has a beat-up body kit, but again I don't really care. In fact, I prefer a car that has a couple dents, dings, and battle scars — it wears its story on its body panels. This isn't a garage queen, it's a car that's really been used the way its engineers and designers intended. That's worth celebrating, and each rock scratch and bit of drift stitching is a celebration in itself.

Are people over 240Ds now? Have they all moved on to J80 Land Cruisers or something? Back in my day, a 240D in this kind of condition for this kind of money would barely last a day on Marketplace or Craigslist, let alone the weeks this one's been on the market. I know, it's not a wagon, but still. It's not gasoline either!

The seller of this particular 240 claims that it not only runs and drives, but has a fairly considerable amount of work done under the hood. The battery, starter, glow plugs, injectors, and fluids are all new. There's also some unspecified "work" on the head, which probably doesn't mean it's been overheated and warped at some point in its history. I'd bet that didn't happen. How would you even overheat a dependable old Volvo diesel like that, even if you wanted to? These things are so bulletproof.

Not every sub-$5,000 car on Facebook Marketplace is an enthusiast icon. I accept that. That doesn't mean that the remainder have to be bad, though — they can be beloved commuter cars with more sporting pretensions than they really need, like this Mazda3. It's no MazdaSpeed, sure, but it's a stick-shift compact sedan with Mazda's jinba ittai philosophy behind its chassis, engine, and suspension design. I think that's pretty good.

This one seems to be in good shape, and the seller certainly claims the same, though it's a little tough to tell what exactly is going on in the photos. They're so smudged, or blurry, or streaked with sun — I can't even tell why they're wrong, I just know that they are. It's still a good car, but damn, Marketplace sellers. Step your photography game up. Or, at least, wipe your phone camera on your shirt before you take your listing photos.

There's been a Prelude parked outside my girlfriend's apartment for a few weeks now, and it looks a lot like this one. Red, not white, but in a similar state of aged-yet-solid — not the cleanest, not the stock-est, but still more than drivable. Well, I assume it's drivable, but it hasn't moved for street sweeping in a while. I hope it's drivable.

This Prelude not only drives, but ought to drive pretty well — it's an Si model, after all. The seller says it's "mechanically pristine" but that the interior needs work, though it looks perfect inside and out to my eye. Maybe I just have lower standards for my car interiors, but this one looks great. All I can see is a bit of work heeded on the sunroof shade, and what might be the tiniest rip in the side of the driver's seat. I don't think either of those are worth addressing with anything more than a bit of gaffer's tape, honestly.

Hey, it's my old bike! Not exactly, mine was a better color, but I did ride a G 310 GS when I first moved to New York and started working at the good ship Jalopnik. I maintain that a baby ADV is secretly the best way to get started on two wheels, provided you're tall enough to manage the seat height —  they can do a bit of everything, and they'll help you figure out where you want to spend your two-wheel time. Try it all on a small adventure bike, then see what you like doing best and cater your next bike towards that.

This particular G 310 GS, though, has one benefit over mine: It's much cheaper. I sold mine for something like $6,000, and this one's asking just $4,000 — surely you can talk the seller down from that. Imagine picking this bike up for a cool $3,500! You'd have a fantastic beginner bike. I got almost too comfortable on mine, riding it sidesaddle and one-legged through Brooklyn traffic, and you could get that same level of comfort on two wheels.

C'mon, I don't need to sell you on this one. A Suzuki Sidekick for under $2,000! Just go buy it.

UnitedHealth Group has sued the federal government over its lowered Medicare Advantage star ratings for next year, further plunging the program’s ratings system into disarray.

UnitedHealth marks at least the 15th Medicare Advantage plan to file a lawsuit against the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services for how the agency calculated 2027 star ratings. The government rates Medicare Advantage plans on a scale from one to five stars, based on health screens, customer satisfaction, and other measures that get mixed into a complicated formula. Those with at least four stars earn bonus money. The insurers argue in their lawsuits that the government’s measurement is inconsistent and is inappropriately dropping their scores below the bonus thresholds.

#5775. Way Before Ducati's Desmo, The Company Started With Puppies

There are few pairings in the motorcycle world more notable than Ducati and Desmo. The famed Italian company is known for making some of the most desirably fast bikes, and so happens to be leading the MotoGP World Championship as of this writing. None of that would be possible, if it weren't for the company's puppies — or rather its Cucciolo engines.

In the midst of World War II, before Vespa began selling its own purpose-built machines to the Italian public to get the country back on the road, Ducati was already in the throes of doing the same. At this time, Ducati was known for its machining and radios, but had decided to try its hand at making an engine. It created a tiny prototype four-stroke cycle engine, paired with a little two-speed gearbox, intended to be affixed to a bicycle to simply give riders a boost of power. The engine's supposed barking-like noise helped inspire its name, Cucciolo, which in Italian means "puppy."

Hearing the "puppy" in action, it doesn't sound much like a puppy. Although the engines demonstrated in these running videos are upwards of 60-80 years old, so they sound like old puppies.

According to Ducati's history, the original Siata factory where the Cucciolo was made had been damaged in the war, and a new factory would open in 1945 to get production rolling. Siata, lastly known as Societa Italiana Applicazioni Tecniche Auto-Aviatorie, did make automobiles, and was tapped to produce Ducati's Cucciolos. In just months demand had outpaced Siata's production capabilities, making at least 240 engines a day, and Ducati moved to take on manufacturing itself.

The Cucciolo would go through three different iterations of the engine, the T2 was a sportier version that had an output of nearly 2 hp and could reach top speeds upwards of 37 mph. The T3 arrived in 1948, featuring a three-speed gearbox. Molto bene!

All of these engines were meant to be installed and mounted onto other bicycles, but Ducati began to see the benefits of doing the same in-house. In 1949, Ducati worked with the airplane manufacturer Caproni to make a tube frame, that could then be paired with the Cucciolo T3 for Ducati's first fully produced motorized bike. Yet the Italian brand's first true complete motorcycle would be the Ducati 60, launched in 1950. It's tiny 60cc engine was another step towards Ducati's famed motorcycle history. Power output was rated for 2 hp at 4500 rpm, with the bike weighing in at 100 pounds. Of course, much like Vespa and Piaggio, Ducati wasted no time in getting into racing and entered its 60 into competition.

Production of Cucciolo engines didn't cease with the making of the 60, but the manufacturing may have changed hands. This 1953 Ducati Cucciolo Rocher Mark IV, on auction with Iconic Motorbikes, was built a few years after the introduction of the Ducati 60. Ducati at this point had allowed other companies to makes its engines, but the Ducati and Cucciolo names remained.

Iconic's particular example was made by Rocher, who according to the auction site, had "built high-end cyclomotors with unique and often extravagant designs. They manufactured Ducati Cucciolo engines with the best materials and cast parts in aluminum rather than using Ducati's inferior high silicon content alloys. This means that damage to Rocher engines can be repaired through welding, which is not possible with Ducati's engines." The switch on Rocher's part makes for an amusing reminder of Ducati's reputation of having engines some individuals believe are difficult to maintain, i.e. the notorious Desmo jokes.

Just a few years after the 60 was created, in 1956, Ducati introduced its first desmodromic valvetrain by putting it into a 125 Grand Prix racing motorcycle. Today its unique but endearing build is featured on many of Ducati's bikes, including most recently, its newly minted motocross bikes. Yet these impressive chariots of speed and the notorious Desmo wouldn't be here, had it not been for the original "puppy."
