#5755. Court Approves $7.25B Settlement With Bayer Over Claims Roundup Caused Cancer

— Some attorneys for patients contend the settlement payouts are too small

Agrochemical maker Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion over two decades to resolve thousands of claims from U.S. cancer patients asserting the company should have warned people that its popular weedkiller Roundup could cause lymphoma, according to a settlement approved Friday by a Missouri judge.

The nationwide settlement applies both to Roundup users who already are ill and those who become diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in future years. Participants could get an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, depending on how they used the product, how old they were when diagnosed, and the severity of their illness.

For Germany-based Bayer, which denies that Roundup causes cancer, the settlement provides some financial certainty against mounting litigation costs that have led it to contemplate pulling the product from U.S. agricultural markets.

Litigants also faced uncertainty. While the settlement was pending, the U.S. Supreme Court undercut one of the central arguments in the Roundup lawsuits. The high court ruled in June that Bayer cannot be sued in state courts on claims it failed to warn about cancer, because federal regulations don't require a cancer warning label and states are forbidden from imposing additional labeling requirements.

Though some attorneys for cancer patients contend the settlement payouts are too small, others argue the deal is better than getting nothing -- which became a heightened likelihood after the Supreme Court ruling.

In a written judgment granting approval, St. Louis Circuit Judge Timothy Boyer said the average individual payouts are "fair and adequate" and the total dollar amount is "among the largest in the history of mass tort personal-injury class action settlements."

Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said in a statement that the court-approved settlement is "a decisive milestone in the company's strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation."

Roundup Has Been Used on Weeds for Over 50 Years

Missouri-based Monsanto debuted Roundup weedkiller in 1974 with the chemical glyphosate as its active ingredient. The product quickly became one of the most widely used herbicides in agriculture. Roundup is designed to be used with genetically modified seeds that can resist the weedkiller's deadly effect, thus allowing farmers to produce more while conserving the soil by tilling it less.

The product also is commonly applied on lawns and gardens.

Bayer added Roundup to its portfolio when it acquired Monsanto in 2018. With it came a growing number of lawsuits alleging glyphosate causes non-Hodgkin lymphoma. But that remains in dispute. The World Health Organization's International Agency for Research on Cancer classified the chemical as "probably carcinogenic" in 2015. The Environmental Protection Agency has determined that it's not likely to cause cancer in humans when used as directed.

About 200,000 Roundup-related claims have been made against Bayer, many coming from people who used it on residential lawns and gardens. As a result, Bayer has removed glyphosate from its new versions of Roundup sold for residential markets.

The lawsuits have produced mixed results. Only a couple dozen cases have gone to jurors, some siding with Bayer and others with plaintiffs. In one case, a Georgia jury awarded plaintiffs $2.1 billion.

In the first Roundup verdict since the Supreme Court's precedent-setting ruling, a Missouri jury in October sided with Bayer in a case alleging design defects, negligence, and fraud. The verdict "should send a strong signal" that plaintiffs "will face significant challenges" pursuing Roundup-related cancer claims in the future, said Bill Dodero, Bayer's U.S. general counsel and global litigation leader.

#5754. CMS to withdraw moratorium on new ACA broker registrations

CMS to withdraw moratorium on new ACA broker registrations" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has agreed to withdraw its moratorium on new broker enrollments, court documents show.

According to a filing submitted Thursday, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Service will published a withdrawal on the Federal Register. The move follows a court ruling earlier this month in favor of two leading organizations representing brokers, which granted a preliminary injunction on the moratorium.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America both sued over the regulation. NABIP argued that the moratorium would have a significant impact on licensed professionals operating in accordance with the law.

Per the document, that stay will remain in place until CMS publishes its withdrawal notice. Once that has been put forth, the plaintiffs will dismiss their complaints as moot. CMS also agreed not to take further action against agents and brokers during the current open enrollment period.

The moratorium, finalized in September, was a part the agency's broader efforts to root out fraud, waste and abuse on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

A federal court has granted a preliminary injunction to two key groups representing insurance brokers over the Trump administration's moratorium on new broker enrollments.

The District Court of Maryland issued the injunction after determining that the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals and Health Agents for America "have shown that they are likely to succeed on the merits of their claims under the Administrative Procedure Act."

The court also said that the organizations made clear they would likely suffer significant harm if the moratorium stays in place.

NABIP said that the ruling means that it will restart training for new brokers beginning on Nov. 6.

"Today’s ruling is a significant victory for licensed agents and brokers and the consumers who rely on their expertise," said NABIP President Mychal Walker in an announcement (PDF). "With Open Enrollment already underway, every day matters."

"Lifting the moratorium immediately and beginning training tomorrow will help affected professionals get to work assisting individuals and families in finding coverage that fits their needs and budgets," said Walker.

NABIP initially sued on Oct. 15 to challenge the moratorium. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services instituted the moratorium in late September as part of its broader push to combat fraud on the Affordable Care Act's exchanges.

The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals is suing the Trump administration over its moratorium on new brokers entering the Affordable Care Act marketplaces.

The organization, the leading trade group for insurance brokers and agents, said the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services' moratorium impacts close to 19,000 brokers and agents who will be barred from registering ahead of open enrollment.

CMS unveiled the moratorium in late September as part of its ongoing push to root out fraud, waste and abuse. In addition, the agency said it would terminate more than 200 agents and brokers that failed to comply with marketplace standards.

The agency said new brokers and agents were disproportionately responsible for submitting inappropriate enrollments and engaging in behaviors at high risk for fraud.

In an announcement (PDF), NABIP says that it supports the broader effort to combat fraud, but that CMS' moratorium "threatens the livelihoods of thousands of legitimate, licensed professionals who have not been accused of fraud and limits consumers’ access to professional assistance as they navigate Open Enrollment."

The organization argues in the lawsuit that the rule instituting the moratorium violates both the Administrative Procedure Act and the Affordable Care Act. The regulation is unlawful as it is "arbitrary, capricious, and unsupported by sufficient evidence," NABIP said.

The 19,000 agents who would be barred from participating under the rule are part of a critical network of professionals who help consumers find coverage that meets their needs, the organization said.

NABIP President Mychal Walker said that CMS should look elsewhere in its fraud efforts.

"The existence of fraud is not in dispute. NABIP has raised these concerns with CMS repeatedly and has offered concrete solutions to address them," Walker said in the announcement. "What is in dispute is whether the appropriate response is to exclude thousands of legitimate agents based solely on whether they registered last year, without any individualized evidence about them."

"There is a better approach: target fraud where it occurs, strengthen the system’s security and hold bad actors accountable while preserving consumers’ access to trusted professionals," Walker continued.

CMS has taken steps to crack down on brokers as the agency views improper ACA enrollments as a key target in its fight against fraud. CMS officials have repeatedly raised concerns that people are enrolled in ACA plans without their knowledge, or despite being deceased.

Earlier this week, the agency revealed it will purge 189,000 enrollees who are currently listed as enrolled in both ACA plans and other coverage, such as Medicaid or Medicare.

#5753. Scientists finally discover why we learn to love bitter coffee

A first taste of black coffee can be surprisingly unpleasant. Its sharp bitterness is the kind of flavor our brains are naturally inclined to avoid. Yet millions of people eventually come to enjoy that same taste, often looking forward to their morning cup. What changes?

Scientists at UC San Francisco may have uncovered an important part of the answer. Their research reveals a little-understood dopamine pathway linking the digestive system and the brain, helping explain how we develop a liking for certain flavors through repeated experience.

Dopamine is a chemical messenger involved in motivation, reward, and learning. Researchers have long known that it helps the brain recognize experiences worth repeating. However, most studies have examined rapid dopamine signals that appear within seconds of encountering something rewarding, such as the sight of a favorite meal.

The new research, published November 4 in Nature, examines a different system. This slower pathway responds to information coming from inside the body, allowing the brain to learn about the benefits of food after it has been consumed.

"We've shown that this slow dopamine system is what drives us to learn to like certain foods over time, and we can see where and how that happens," said Zachary Knight, PhD, professor of Physiology and senior author of the study.

The findings offer a possible explanation for why an initially unpleasant flavor can gradually become enjoyable. Once the brain connects the taste of coffee with caffeine's stimulating effects, Knight explained, "that coffee starts to taste a lot better."

How the Gut Sends Reward Signals to the Brain

Scientists have spent decades investigating dopamine and its influence on behavior. Its familiar, rapidly acting signals help us respond to opportunities for reward. But dopamine also operates on a slower timescale, through a system that has received far less attention.

According to Knight, this slower process largely unfolds outside our conscious awareness.

When food enters the digestive tract, specialized sensors detect nutrients, including sugar and fat. Information about those nutrients travels toward the brain, where it can produce a dopamine response that develops gradually and continues for several minutes.

To investigate this process, Knight worked with James Grove, PhD, who was a graduate student at the time. They introduced nutrients directly into the stomachs of mice while monitoring dopamine activity throughout their brains.

The researchers used either sugar water or a liquid resembling a milkshake. Delivering these substances directly into the stomach allowed them to separate the effects of nutrients from the experience of tasting food.

The results revealed a powerful, prolonged dopamine response in a specific brain region called the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA.

The amygdala is involved in emotional processing and learning, including forming associations between experiences and their consequences. Scientists already knew that dopamine was released in this particular region, but its purpose had remained unclear.

"We could see that this dopamine is part of a different system and begin to understand its role," he said.

Scientists Find a Brain Circuit That Changes Food Preferences

Finding the dopamine signal was only the beginning. The researchers next wanted to determine whether it actually influenced how animals learned to prefer different flavors.

They first interrupted the newly identified pathway in mice. The animals continued eating normally, indicating that the disruption did not prevent them from consuming food. However, they lost the ability to learn that an unfamiliar flavor was associated with receiving calories.

The team then conducted the opposite experiment.

After mice tasted a flavor containing no calories, the researchers artificially activated dopamine fibers in the BLA. Remarkably, the animals developed a preference for that flavor even though it provided no nutritional reward.

In effect, stimulating the pathway reproduced the learning signal that nutrients would ordinarily generate.

Together, the experiments showed that this dopamine system plays a critical role in teaching the brain which flavors predict rewarding nutritional effects.

A Surprising Discovery in the Left Side of the Brain

The researchers also looked for evidence that a comparable process occurs in humans. Brain imaging studies conducted by Knight's collaborators revealed a strikingly similar pattern.

Dana Small, PhD, a psychologist at Yale University, revisited data from an earlier positron emission tomography (PET) study involving 13 men. Participants had consumed either a milkshake or a drink without calories.

Her analysis found that dopamine release following nutrient delivery was especially concentrated in the left side of the BLA.

A separate study led by Marc Tittgemeyer, PhD, and his colleagues provided additional evidence. Using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in brain activity associated with blood flow, the researchers examined 38 adults after they consumed glucose, a simple sugar.

They observed increased activity in the same brain region.

One of the most unexpected findings was that the response was not evenly distributed between the brain's two hemispheres.

In both mice and humans, nutrients produced a considerably stronger dopamine response in the left BLA than in the corresponding region on the right.

That imbalance surprised Knight because brain networks responsible for essential functions, such as feeding, are generally expected to work in a relatively symmetrical fashion.

Why the left side plays such a prominent role remains unanswered. Knight's laboratory is now investigating what causes this unusual difference.

Could This Discovery Help Scientists Change Food Cravings?

Identifying the pathway provides researchers with a clearer picture of how the digestive system influences the brain's learned responses to food. It also raises an intriguing possibility: Could scientists eventually use this knowledge to change which foods people find appealing?

One area of interest involves GLP-1 medications, a class of drugs that mimic a hormone naturally released by the gut. These medications can substantially alter appetite and eating behavior.

Knight's team did not investigate GLP-1 drugs in the new study, so it remains unknown whether they influence the dopamine pathway the researchers identified.

Still, Knight suggests that one possible explanation for some of their effects could involve reducing the dopamine signals generated when nutrients reach the digestive system. If that happens, foods might gradually become less rewarding because the brain would receive weaker signals reinforcing their flavors.

For now, this remains a hypothesis rather than a demonstrated effect of the medications.

The broader implications extend beyond hunger and fullness. Many approaches to changing eating behavior focus on reducing appetite or increasing feelings of satisfaction after a meal. The newly mapped pathway suggests that the brain's process of learning food preferences could eventually become another target.

By influencing how the brain connects flavors with their consequences, future treatments might someday help people develop different preferences rather than simply making them feel less hungry.

"By understanding the steps between nutrient detection in the gut and learning in the brain, it might be possible to fine-tune them to subtly change our preferences for different foods," Knight said.

The discovery offers a new perspective on why our tastes can change over time. From learning to enjoy bitter coffee to developing a preference for calorie-rich foods, what we love to eat may depend partly on a quiet conversation between the gut and brain that continues long after the first bite.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-DK106399, R01-DK138127, R01-NS116626, and R01-DK145100 and F31-NS120468).

Isabella is a chronic disease reporter writing about how the Trump administration is tackling the nation’s health epidemic — or not. You can reach her on Signal at isabellacueto.03.

WASHINGTON — Department of Health and Human Services officials announced Friday that 15 groups around the U.S. will test how well nutrition, exercise, and other lifestyle programs work to improve Medicare patients’ health and save the government money.

The MAHA ELEVATE program aims to generate evidence over the next several years that preventive efforts, such as cooking classes and nutrition coaching for people with chronic conditions, is worthy of Medicare coverage.

The U.S. spends trillions of dollars per year on health care, most of which goes toward treating chronic diseases. However, Medicare does not cover many of the lifestyle interventions that could help people improve their condition or keep them from getting sick in the first place.

#5750. UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings

UnitedHealth the latest insurer to sue over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

UnitedHealth Group is joining the ranks of insurers that are suing the feds over the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings calculations.

Much like other recent lawsuits, the healthcare giant argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services inappropriately used multiple measures in the calculations. Over the summer, a Georgia federal court sided with MA plan Clover Health, and tossed 20 measures that were used in its 2026 scores.

That legal ruling has been the basis of much of the current round of legal wrangling.

UnitedHealth said in its complaint that it is bringing the lawsuit to ensure "that their 2027 Star Ratings are calculated in accordance with CMS’s statutory authority and procedural obligations."

The star ratings are tied to quality bonus payments for Medicare Advantage plans and listed on the Medicare plan finder to help individuals identify high-quality coverage. When those payments are lower due to a decline in scores, the insurer may not be as nimble in lowering premiums or enhancing benefits.

"The Star Ratings carry real consequences," UnitedHealth wrote in the complaint. "A plan’s Star Rating thus directly affects the benefits and healthcare offerings that Medicare beneficiaries receive."

Elevance Health is the latest insurer to sue the feds over its performance in the latest round of star ratings for the Medicare Advantage program.

The company sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services in District of Columbia federal court on Friday, arguing that the 2027 star ratings calculations violated the Administrative Procedure Act in using 11 measures that it says were adopted unlawfully.

In the lawsuit, the company said that the harm from including these measures is "concrete and substantial." If they were excluded, it would increase the scores for 12 of its Medicare Advantage contracts and generate $516 million in additional quality bonus payments.

"Their inclusion therefore does more than violate statutory requirements in the abstract: it depresses Elevance Health’s ratings and reduces the funding available for the following payment year," per the lawsuit. "That funding could support broader supplemental benefits, lower premiums and cost-sharing, and improved care coordination."

"CMS’s unlawful methodology puts those resources out of reach," the company said.

In addition to the financial impacts, Elevance argues that the star ratings scores can also lead to reputational damage that makes it harder for them to compete in the MA market. It also provides prospective enrollees with inaccurate information, the company said.

"Beneficiaries cannot make informed coverage choices when the government’s own comparison tool conveys a distorted assessment of the plans available to them," Elevance said.

"An artificially depressed rating does not merely place Elevance Health at a competitive disadvantage; it undermines the very comparison the program is supposed to enable," the company continued. "A rating lowered by unlawful measures presents beneficiaries with a misleading signal of relative quality, rather than a lawful basis for distinguishing among competing plans."

CVS Heath's Aetna is joining the ranks of insurers suing over its results in the 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

The insured filed suit Monday in Georgia's Southern District Court, and argues that 28 measures used by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services to calculate its scores were "unlawfully adopted" and should have been excluded.

The court is the same venue that ruled in favor of Clover Health over the summer, and set aside 20 measures that were used to determine its 2026 scores. That decision, which the feds have appealed, kicked off a broad recalculation of 2026 scores that looked different for insurers outside of Clover, triggering a wave of litigation.

In its lawsuit, Aetna cites the Clover decision in finding that CMS extended beyond its statutory authority in deploying those 20 measures.

The company said that calculating its scores using the 28 measures in question will likely cost it $2 billion in 2028 quality bonus payments and rebate retention. Those are funds that the insurer could "apply toward expanding member benefits, reducing premiums and investing in quality improvement."

Aetna adds that in addition to the monetary loss, having lower scores negatively impacts the company's reputation and its ability to attract potential members.

"The harm to CVS Health is not exclusively financial; lower ratings carry meaningful reputational harm, which can in turn impact membership," per the lawsuit. "By incorporating unlawful measures into the 2027 Star Ratings calculation, CMS cast CVS Health’s ratings in a poorer light in the eyes of Medicare Advantage consumers relative to peer MAOs, undermining CVS Health’s ability to compete for Medicare beneficiaries through enhanced benefits and the like."

Aetna did not respond to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Based on an analysis from Stephens, 69% of Aetna's MA members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 81%. That threshold is the key to securing quality bonus payments.

Aetna's complaint follows others focused on the 2027 scores from Centene and Alignment Healthcare (see those stories below).

Centene has become the latest insurer to sue the federal government over its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings.

In a lawsuit filed Thursday in Georgia's Southern District Court, the company argues that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services violated the Administrative Procedure Act in determining its latest scores. Centene says that CMS ran afoul of "core statutory safeguards" in deploying 17 measures.

The use of those measures ultimately caused "significant injury" to the company, according to the complaint. For 2027, 9% of Centene's members are enrolled in plans with at least four stars, which declined from 18% in the prior year.

"In implementing each of the individual Star measures that Centene challenges, CMS violated applicable law and thereby caused Centene to lose out on hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that Centene could use to strengthen benefits, reduce premiums, and improve health outcomes," the company said in the lawsuit.

CMS argues that the court has already sided with a similar argument in its decision in favor of Clover Health earlier this year. In that case, which led to a broad recalculation in scores, the courts set aside 20 measures that were used in determining Clover's star ratings for 2026.

If the 17 measures in question had been excluded in calculating Centene's scores, the company estimates it would receive $448 million more in quality bonus payments for the 2028 plan year, funds it would deploy to expand benefits, lower premiums and enhance programs like care coordination.

In addition to the financial impact, a drop in star ratings also carries a reputational hit, Centene said.

"Beyond the financial impact to the company and its members, depressed ratings also inflict significant reputational damage and diminished membership," the company said in the complaint

Centene had not returned a request for comment at the time of publication.

Alignment Healthcare sued federal regulators, alleging that its 2027 Medicare Advantage star ratings were determined "in flagrant violation" of statute.

In the lawsuit filed Friday in District of Columbia federal court, the insurer says that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services "has completely departed from Congress’s vision of leveraging predictable, valid measures developed with input from providers, plans, and the public" in establishing the methodology for the star ratings.

The company argues that rather than establish "consistent, stable specifications" for metrics through the traditional rule-making process, the agency instead detailed key measures through a series of "technical notes." This violates the Administrative Procedure Act, per the lawsuit.

The program's star ratings are the critical determinant in quality bonus payments to insurers as well as a tool that aims to make it easier for enrollees and brokers to identify benefits with the highest quality.

"Consistent application of the statutory requirements governing Star Ratings is therefore essential not only to plan payments and competition but also to ensuring that beneficiaries can rely on the Star Ratings as meaningful and comparable measures of plan quality," Alignment said in the lawsuit.

The company adds that multiple recent court decisions have set aside CMS' star ratings methodology, notably a ruling over the summer in favor of Clover Health that tossed 20 metrics used in the 2026 calculations. A Georgia federal judge determined that 10 measures utilized exceeded CMS' authority, while 10 other measures were promulgated inappropriately.

CMS recalculated the scores across the board following the ruling, but only set aside the 10 measures that the courts determined were outside the bounds of its regulatory authority. The agency maintained that approach in the 2027 calculations, Alignment argues.

"Congress created the Star Ratings program to allow Medicare Advantage beneficiaries to make informed decisions about plan enrollment based on clinically validated measures of plan quality that had been subjected to notice and comment," the company said. "CMS’s contrary approach fails to carry out the vision that Congress set forth by statute."

The Trump administration has appealed the Clover decision, so that legal case remains ongoing.

In addition, Alignment argues it suffered reputational and financial damage as a result of its 2027 scores, which plummeted compared to the prior year. Just 25% of its members are in plans with four or more stars for 2027, down from 100% in 2026.

Shares in the company tumbled following the release of the ratings, though stock prices have rebounded since.

Alignment sued the feds following the Clover decision to secure a recalculation for its scores that aligns with the court's decision, and in a statement to Fierce Healthcare, said that the lawsuit aligns with that perspective.

"Our lawsuit seeks to ensure that the Star Ratings program operates as Congress intended and that Alignment is properly compensated for the care we provide," Alignment said in the statement. "We respect the judicial process and will present our case in court. Because this matter involves pending litigation, we will not comment on the specific legal arguments beyond our filings."

"Our focus remains on delivering exceptional care, improving health outcomes and advocating for a stable, lawful regulatory framework that supports seniors and strengthens the Medicare Advantage program," the company said.

Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was launched in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

To break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it says. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

Furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. #5748. Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain

Alzheimer's disease is best known for its effects on memory and thinking, but new research suggests that some symptoms may develop in a surprising place: outside the brain.

Scientists at the University of Central Florida (UCF) have discovered that genetic mutations associated with Alzheimer's can interfere with the nerves that control muscle movement, even without involvement from the brain or spinal cord. The findings could help explain why some people with Alzheimer's experience changes in walking, balance, or coordination long before noticeable memory problems emerge.

The discovery raises the possibility that movement difficulties could provide earlier warning signs of the disease and that treatments focused exclusively on the brain may overlook important problems elsewhere in the body.

The research was led by James Hickman, a professor at UCF's Nanoscience Technology Center, and Research Professor Xiufang "Nadine" Guo, working alongside scientists at the healthcare technology company Hesperos. Funded by the National Institutes of Health's National Institute on Aging, the study used laboratory systems built from human cells to investigate how inherited Alzheimer's mutations affect movement. The findings were published in Alzheimer's & Dementia: The Journal of the Alzheimer's Association.

"Motor deficits may be an earlier indication [of Alzheimer's]," Guo says. "If we can detect those changes and intervene earlier, that could help delay the onset of central nervous system symptoms."

Why Alzheimer's Symptoms May Appear Before Memory Loss

Alzheimer's is generally associated with progressive memory loss, confusion, and declining cognitive abilities. However, doctors have also observed that some patients develop physical symptoms, including changes in balance, coordination, and gait (manner of walking), years before clear cognitive difficulties become apparent.

These observations have raised an important question: Are such movement problems simply a consequence of damage occurring in the brain, or could Alzheimer's also interfere directly with nerves elsewhere in the body?

To investigate, the UCF team focused on familial Alzheimer's, a rare inherited form of the disease that typically develops earlier in life (from 40 to 65 years of age) than the more common form.

Their experiments revealed that motor neurons carrying mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's could disrupt the connections responsible for controlling muscles, even when the brain and spinal cord were completely absent from the experimental system.

Motor neurons are specialized nerve cells that transmit signals to muscles, telling them when to contract and produce movement. The new findings suggest that Alzheimer's mutations can interfere with this process directly, rather than affecting movement only through damage to the brain.

"This is the first time it's been demonstrated that deficits in the peripheral nervous system can arise directly from these mutations," Hickman says. "It means drugs that target the brain may not fix problems in the rest of the body."

The peripheral nervous system includes the nerves located outside the brain and spinal cord. These nerves carry signals between the central nervous system and the rest of the body, helping control movement, sensation, and other essential functions.

Guo also points out that preserving the ability to move could have benefits beyond physical health. Regular physical activity is associated with better cognitive well-being, so protecting motor function may also help support brain health.

How a Miniature Human Cell System Revealed the Discovery

To examine the relationship between Alzheimer's mutations and muscle movement, the scientists used an innovative laboratory platform known as "human-on-a-chip" technology.

Developed and manufactured through Hesperos, a company co-founded by Hickman, these miniature systems bring different types of human cells together under controlled conditions. They allow researchers to recreate specific biological functions and observe how diseases interfere with them.

Unlike conventional laboratory experiments that examine isolated cells, these systems can reproduce important interactions between different tissues. They also provide an alternative to animal models, which do not always accurately reflect how human diseases behave.

For this study, the team created a miniature model of the neuromuscular junction, the connection where a motor neuron communicates with a muscle cell.

The model was deliberately designed without a brain or spinal cord. This was a crucial part of the experiment because it allowed the researchers to investigate whether Alzheimer's-related changes could cause movement problems independently of the central nervous system.

The scientists combined healthy muscle cells with motor neurons derived from stem cells that carried genetic mutations associated with familial Alzheimer's disease. Stem cells are cells that can develop into specialized types of cells, making them valuable tools for studying human diseases in the laboratory.

The researchers then examined how effectively the altered nerve cells communicated with otherwise healthy muscle tissue.

The results showed that the Alzheimer's-associated mutations could interfere with normal nerve-to-muscle function. This suggests that at least some movement difficulties linked to the disease may arise directly in the peripheral nervous system rather than being caused entirely by degeneration in the brain.

Why Damaged Nerve Connections Can Affect Walking and Balance

Every voluntary movement depends on successful communication between the nervous system and the muscles.

At the neuromuscular junction, an electrical signal traveling along a motor neuron triggers chemical communication that causes a muscle to contract. This process makes everyday activities possible, from walking and maintaining posture to lifting objects and performing precise movements.

When the connection becomes impaired, muscles may respond less effectively to nerve signals. Depending on the severity and location of the problem, this can contribute to weakness, reduced coordination, and difficulty sustaining physical activity.

To evaluate these effects, the research team measured how consistently nerve signals produced muscle contractions and how long the muscles could continue contracting before becoming fatigued.

These measurements provided a direct assessment of how well the nerve and muscle cells worked together. They also resemble aspects of the functional testing physicians use when examining patients with movement disorders.

"You can't move unless the motor circuit works," Hickman says. "When a doctor taps your knee to check your reflex, they're testing that exact connection."

By demonstrating impaired nerve-to-muscle communication in a system containing no brain or spinal cord, the study provides evidence that mutations linked to familial Alzheimer's can produce effects beyond the central nervous system.

However, the experiments do not establish that these changes necessarily occur before memory loss in patients. Further research will be needed to determine how closely the laboratory findings reflect the progression of Alzheimer's in people, particularly those with the more common forms of the disease.

Could This Discovery Lead to Earlier Alzheimer's Detection?

The findings suggest a potentially important new direction for Alzheimer's research: looking beyond memory and other cognitive symptoms when investigating the disease.

If future studies confirm that changes in motor function are detectable early in certain patients, tests of walking, coordination, or nerve-to-muscle activity might eventually help identify disease-related changes before more obvious neurological symptoms develop.

The results also raise questions about treatment. Many Alzheimer's therapies are designed to address processes occurring in the brain, but medications that target the central nervous system may not necessarily correct abnormalities affecting peripheral nerves and muscles.

Understanding these separate effects could help researchers investigate treatments that protect physical function alongside cognitive health.

Human-on-a-Chip Technology Could Transform Disease Research

Beyond the implications for Alzheimer's, the researchers see considerable potential in using human-on-a-chip systems to investigate other diseases and evaluate possible treatments.

Because these platforms contain human cells and reproduce measurable biological activities, they can help scientists observe disease-related changes in conditions that more closely resemble human physiology than some conventional experimental models.

This approach may be particularly useful in drug development, where researchers need to understand not only how a potential treatment affects individual cells but also how it influences interactions between different tissues.

Such systems can also uncover biological effects that may be difficult to detect in animal experiments, potentially helping researchers identify promising therapies and recognize limitations earlier in development.

For Hickman, the progress represents the culmination of three decades of work devoted to understanding disease through more realistic laboratory models.

"These systems let us study disease in a way that's closer to what actually happens in the human body, and that's what we need to develop better treatments," he says.

#5747. STAT+: Is MAHA’s think tank in the tank? Tax filings show low reserves

Isabella is a chronic disease reporter writing about how the Trump administration is tackling the nation’s health epidemic — or not. You can reach her on Signal at isabellacueto.03.

WASHINGTON —The MAHA Institute, a nonprofit “think tank” launched to support Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s health agenda, burned over $1 million in 2025, leaving it with little cash on hand to continue operating, tax documents obtained by STAT show.

The group started 2025 with nearly $1.3 million in its coffers, but ended the year with just $171,000, per its latest IRS return, filed this week. That 86% drop was hardly offset by the group’s revenue, which was just shy of $67,000 for the year.

“To have lost over $1 million is pretty notable to me,” said Brian Mittendorf, a professor at Ohio State University who specializes in nonprofit accounting.

#5746. CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition

CMS issues Medicare Advantage proposals aimed at boosting competition" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has proposed a slew of changes to Medicare Advantage and Part D designed to "revitalize care" in these markets.

For one, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said late Friday that it will update application and network adequacy requirements to make it easier for new entrants. The agency proposed to require organizations to demonstrate network adequacy during their first year in operation, rather than during the application process.

This shift would eliminate a significant barrier for new entrants, driving greater competition in the market.

CMS has also proposed combining three specialty areas in behavioral health — clinical psychology, clinical social work and outpatient behavioral health — into one specialty group for the purposes of network adequacy. The changes will give plans greater flexibility in building out behavioral health networks.

CMS will also make adjustments that seek to boost competition for special needs plans.

In addition, the agency said it will make adjustments to the star ratings program, focusing its ratings on 15 measures. The proposed measure set would emphasize "clinical outcomes and patient experience while retaining select process measures in high-priority areas where performance remains low."

CMS is also aiming to update the calculation methodology that will "raise the bar for achieving high ratings," and thus quality bonus payments.

"People with Medicare should be able to choose coverage based on what matters most to them — quality, affordability, and access," said CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz, M.D., in the announcement. "These proposals are about creating a Medicare Advantage marketplace that rewards better care and better value while empowering beneficiaries with the options and knowledge they need to make informed decisions about their health."

The proposed rule also includes provisions that align with Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy's Make America Healthy Again agenda by setting a "healthy food" standard that MA plans should follow for supplemental benefits.

The goal, CMS said, is to ensure that Medicare dollars are spent on food benefits that align with MAHA.

"Medicare food benefits should pay for nutritious food that helps people improve their health and manage chronic disease," Kennedy said in the announcement. "This proposal would require those benefits to meet the Dietary Guidelines for Americans while preserving access to foods and nutritional products that providers recommend for patients’ specific medical needs."

"Under President Trump, we are putting prevention at the center of health care and demanding more from every Medicare dollar," Kennedy said.

#5745. ICE detention of Princeton scientist rattles academia

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

Anil Oza is a general assignment reporter at STAT focused on the NIH and health equity. You can reach him on Signal at aniloza.16.

A graduate student who is a scientific researcher at Princeton University was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement earlier this week while traveling home after presenting research at the annual Society for Neuroscience conference in Washington, D.C.

The researcher, Eva Yi Xie, was detained Thursday. Although she has lived in the U.S. since 2016 after moving to the country from China, her visa had expired, according to The New York Times. Her lawyers told a reporter Xie had a pending asylum application and was thus allowed to remain in the country legally.

The news, first posted by a mentor of Xie’s on X, ricocheted across academic circles on Friday, in part because it seemed to crystalize pervasive fears of non-U.S. academics and international students that traveling to conferences to present new research and network with colleagues may be too risky during a second Trump administration that has cracked down on immigration.

“There’s, I think, an open question about whether or not it’s safe for people who are international students on visas to travel, because there have been these detentions, and that’s a very scary prospect,” said Caitlin Rivers, a John Hopkins academic who said a staff member of hers was detained by ICE earlier this year. A number of U.S. conferences have reported smaller attendance over the past two years, and some have considered hosting in other countries.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment as to why Xie was detained. But the administration has been vocal in its desire to reduce the number of foreign-born graduate students in the U.S. In its science blueprint released earlier this year, the White House wrote “America’s over-reliance on foreign students also creates a security challenge.”

Xie is not the first graduate student to be detained. In one notable instance, Tufts researcher Rumeysa Ozturk was detained by ICE last year in Cambridge, Mass., and later decided to leave the country. A report released earlier this week found that international graduate student enrollment is down by a third at academic medical centers.

“News of Eva’s detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” Rodney D. Priestley, the dean of Princeton University’s graduate school, wrote in a statement, adding the university has provided Xie with legal representation. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”

Xie’s work lies at the intersection of neuroscience and artificial intelligence; she uses a combination of experiments on mice and large datasets of neural recordings to understand how different portions of the brain work together to make decisions. A third-year PhD student, she is viewed as a rising star by some of her colleagues.

“I think it speaks to how exceptional of a researcher Eva is that she can work on projects that really span multiple disciplines, that require that she go and learn the foundations, not just of AI and machine learning, and not just computational models of the brain, but also understanding how do you run the experiment on the mice. She’s in the lab actually doing the surgery on the mice, gathering the data from the mice, analyzing those data, and running the AI experiments,” said Benjamin Eysenbach, a computer scientist at Princeton and one of Xie’s advisers.

As an example of the respect she commands among peers, Eysenbach cited a workshop she convened at last year’s NeurIPS conference, one of the premiere machine learning conferences. Xie presented research of her own, and also brought together leaders in AI and in neuroscience to see how they could collaborate.

It was an opportunity both to “introduce these important questions about the brain to folks in AI that might be equipped with new methods, and to help folks working on neuroscience questions define what are the right AI tools,” Eysenbach said.

Krithik Ramesh, a fellow researcher, is among those who has benefitted from her guidance. The two had overlapped at science fair competitions throughout high school, and when Ramesh was considering transferring to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where Xie had completed her undergraduate degree, he turned to her for counsel. He learned about Xie’s detention after a friend saw a post on social media. His immediate reaction was disbelief, followed by a sense of unmooring as a fellow researcher.

“We academics exist for the benefit of the public,” he said. “We are very privileged as a country to have people like Eva continue to pursue academia at the highest level, and to share that with other people. That’s literally the nature and reason why we go to conferences to present stuff. It is appalling to me that she cannot do that with reasonable certainty that she can’t be detained.”

#5744. Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia

A surprising new study has found that people who are overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia tend to live longer than those who have a normal body weight. The findings challenge expectations about the relationship between weight and health, suggesting that carrying extra weight may be associated with an unexpected survival advantage after dementia develops.

Researchers from Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and NYU School of Global Public Health found that body weight at the time of diagnosis may provide important clues about how long someone with dementia is likely to live. Their findings, published in the Journal of Alzheimer's Disease, also highlight the importance of proper nutrition for people living with the condition.

The results are particularly intriguing because obesity is well established as a risk factor for several serious health problems, including heart disease and diabetes. Being overweight or obese during middle age is also associated with a greater likelihood of developing dementia later in life. However, previous research has suggested that the relationship may reverse once dementia has developed, with higher body weight linked to better survival.

"Because this finding is somewhat counterintuitive, an important question is whether it could simply be an artifact of bias. Our analyses suggest that the major sources of bias we examined do not explain the survival advantage associated with higher weight," said corresponding author Yuan Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of Sociomedical Sciences at Columbia Mailman and in the Butler Columbia Aging Center.

Obesity Linked to Up to 27% Lower Risk of Death

The researchers found substantial differences in survival based on body weight at the time of dementia diagnosis. Compared with individuals in the normal weight range, those who were overweight or obese had a significantly lower risk of death, even after the researchers accounted for smoking, existing medical conditions, and demographic characteristics.

People classified as overweight (body mass index of 25 to 29.9) had a 16 percent lower risk of death. Those with class 1 obesity (BMI of 30 to 34.9) had an even larger reduction of 27 percent, while individuals with class 2 and 3 obesity (BMI equal to or greater than 35) had a 22 percent lower risk.

Despite these striking differences, the researchers caution that the findings should not be interpreted as a recommendation for people with dementia to gain weight.

"This doesn't mean that patients with dementia should attempt to become overweight or obese, as our study was not designed to test that question. But our findings do suggest that weight status may serve as a useful prognostic signal for survival at the time of dementia diagnosis. They also support the notion that nutrition is a key factor in the health and survival of people with dementia," said Virginia Chang, associate professor of Social and Behavioral Sciences at NYU School of Global Public Health and the study's first author.

Tracking Weight and Dementia Over 24 Years

To investigate the connection, Zhang, Chang, and their colleagues examined information from the Health and Retirement Study, a nationally representative research project that follows Americans ages 51 and older.

The team analyzed records collected between 1998 and 2022, focusing on 4,523 participants who did not have dementia when they entered the study but subsequently developed the condition.

Because the data covered such a long period, the researchers could examine how participants' weight changed in the years leading up to their diagnosis. They could also determine their weight when dementia was identified and track their survival afterward.

This extended timeline was especially important because scientists have questioned whether the apparent benefit of higher body weight is genuine or simply reflects misleading patterns in the data. One possibility is that having additional fat or muscle gives patients resources that help them withstand the physical effects of dementia. Another is that the association arises from factors that earlier studies did not adequately consider.

Could Weight Loss Explain the Dementia Paradox?

One major concern involves weight loss that occurs before dementia becomes clinically apparent.

Earlier research by Zhang and Chang found that people can begin losing weight as much as 10 years before a dementia diagnosis, with the decline becoming more pronounced as the disease approaches.

This creates a potential problem for studies that measure weight only at the time dementia is diagnosed. Some individuals classified as having a normal weight may previously have been heavier and lost weight because of the developing disease. If those individuals are already experiencing more advanced illness, they may face a greater risk of death, making higher body weight appear beneficial by comparison.

The researchers also considered other possible distortions. Restricting an analysis to people who develop dementia can create misleading relationships between obesity and mortality, even when the underlying connection is more complicated.

Another concern is known as "survivor" bias. Since people with obesity face an increased risk of dying from certain illnesses before reaching the age when dementia typically develops, those who survive long enough to receive a dementia diagnosis may represent an unusually healthy group.

To determine whether these factors explained the findings, the team performed additional analyses designed to evaluate several potential sources of bias. The results indicated that the biases they examined were unlikely to be major drivers of the observed connection between higher weight and lower mortality.

Why Extra Weight Might Help People With Dementia

Although the precise explanation remains unknown, the researchers identified several biological reasons why additional body weight could be advantageous for someone already living with dementia.

One possibility involves the body's energy reserves. People with more stored fat or greater muscle mass may be better equipped to withstand periods of poor nutrition and the physical deterioration that can accompany the disease.

Dementia can interfere with eating in several ways. Changes in brain function may reduce appetite or motivation to eat, while some patients experience increased energy needs or gradually lose the ability to feed themselves. Over time, these problems can contribute to significant weight loss, muscle wasting, and declining health.

"Nutrition can be a big problem for people with dementia," said Chang. "They may experience wasting and an inability to eat, which can be due to changes in the brain's central drive, leading to loss of appetite and initiative, increased energy expenditure, and difficulties feeding themselves."

Having additional energy stores or muscle tissue could potentially help patients cope with these challenges, although the study did not establish that these factors directly explain the survival differences.

The researchers emphasize that important questions remain unanswered. Even after examining multiple potential biases and identifying plausible biological explanations, they cannot say for certain why overweight and obese participants experienced lower mortality.

Nevertheless, Zhang and Chang believe that weight at the time of a dementia diagnosis could provide valuable information about a patient's likely survival. The results also reinforce the importance of recognizing and addressing nutritional problems in people with dementia.

Additional study authors include Eleanor Hayes-Larson of the University of Southern California and Hui Zheng of the University of Toronto.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grant numbers R00AG070274, R00AG075317).

#5743. Superhuman unveils personal AI assistant and expands Go across entire suite

Superhuman Inc., formerly known as Grammarly, today announced the expansion of Go, its proactive artificial intelligence assistant and multi-agent platform, along with updated features across its entire suite.

Among the updates, the company added a new personalized AI assistant in Go that users can name, give work to and ask to watch projects and to-do lists in the background. The new assistant will work across connected tools, suggest next steps, draft content in the user’s voice, and manage a team of other AI agents, with the user always in the loop.

Superhuman also brought agents into Docs and Mail and updated Fathom, the company’s note-taking app, to act as a collaborative, bot-free app that connects natively to every application across the Superhuman suite and captures video, screen sharing, and audio.

“Superhuman is solving for the last mile of AI: the gap between deployment and adoption,” said Chief Executive Shishir Mehrotra. “The best AI shows up for your whole team, not just the power users who go looking for it. It’s embedded in the tools you already use, it works ahead of you, and it collaborates alongside you.”

Superhuman Go is growing with a personal agent that works ahead of a user on their behalf, with their approval. The company said the new Go assistant acts like an extra set of eyes and ears, watching out for users throughout their day, finding tasks they need to do, and keeping up with their “need to know.” It tries to stay ahead of their task list, offers to complete things it can, picks up slack, summarizes meeting notes, and answers important emails or preps for important meetings.

It also writes like the user and gets better over time with direction. It learns from past responses to draft content that sounds like them, refines writing before they hit send, and keeps learning their style to improve over time.

Superhuman said that it added more than 20 new partner agents, which can help pull in expert knowledge and capabilities from enterprise services. For example, a user can connect to Legora AB’s agent for legal intelligence, Databricks Inc.’s Live Metrics agent for metrics and relevant numbers, Amplitude Inc.’s Product check agent to verify product usage claims, and Blackboard Inc.’s Assignment Coach agent to help students improve coursework.

With the rise of personal AI agents such as OpenClaw and Meta Platform Inc.’s Muse, the open-source community, startups and enterprises have begun offering personalized agents that autonomously assist users with day-to-day tasks and work. Anthropic PBC also recently launched Claude Duet, a similar proactive AI agent for professionals and small businesses in private preview, that completes tasks when asked and keeps working in the background.

Superhuman Go agents are now native in Docs, the company’s AI-native collaborative workspace that combines documents, spreadsheets and automated workflows. Users can share a doc with any agent, just mentioning it with @ to hand off work, and it will show up as another collaborator.

Users can add agents with triggers for when to run, and they will interact with the document whether it’s open or not, updating it whenever something changes. This will allow agents to collaborate by adding to the document and changing it by checking email, watching connected apps or checking connected tables, so that the information in the doc stays fresh.

Similarly, agents connect to Mail and every other tool. This means that when drafting an email, agents can suggest content as users type. Superhuman Mail can use agents to pull in information from Slack, meeting notes or internal documents. The company said auto drafts already saves users an average of nine minutes per draft. For a user who replies to four emails a day, that can save about three hours a week.

In addition to these changes, Superhuman said the Go platform software development kit is generally available to partners and customers with new agent-building capabilities. Partners can now easily build and connect their own agents that show up anywhere within Go. The company plans to add more specialized partner agents.

#5742. STAT+: FDA rejects Capricor Therapeutics’ Duchenne therapy, a decision that was a long time coming

Adam Feuerstein is a senior writer and biotech columnist, reporting on the crossroads of drug development, business, Wall Street, and biotechnology. He is also a co-host of the weekly biotech podcast The Readout Loud and author of the newsletter Adam’s Biotech Scorecard. You can reach Adam on Signal at stataf.54.

The Food and Drug Administration said Friday that it had rejected a cell therapy intended for patients with Duchenne muscular dystrophy developed by Capricor Therapeutics.

The decision to block the treatment, called deramiocel, from reaching the market should have been an easy one for regulators to make. The targeted patient population — teenagers and young men with Duchenne who had already lost the ability to walk — have few treatment options today. Deramiocel didn’t help them either. Capricor conducted two randomized clinical trials. Both failed to show deramiocel could stave off heart failure or preserve muscle function in their arms.

But nothing is straightforward when it comes to regulating drugs for Duchenne, a progressive, muscle-wasting disease.

#5740. Why heart attacks can still happen even when bad cholesterol is low

Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have uncovered new clues about why some people develop heart disease even after lowering their bad cholesterol to recommended levels. Their findings point to biological processes involving other fat-carrying particles in the blood that may contribute to cardiovascular damage in ways that go beyond cholesterol buildup. By identifying these previously poorly understood mechanisms, the research could help pave the way for more targeted strategies to prevent heart disease and potentially save lives.

Heart disease remains one of the world's leading causes of death. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), cardiovascular diseases kill nearly 17.9 million people worldwide each year, with heart attacks and strokes responsible for more than 80% of those deaths. Coronary heart disease develops when fatty deposits containing cholesterol (cholesterol) build up inside the arteries that supply blood to the heart. If left untreated, the condition can eventually cause a heart attack.

Reducing LDL cholesterol, commonly known as "bad cholesterol," is a proven way to lower the likelihood of a heart attack. However, bringing LDL cholesterol into the recommended range does not eliminate the danger. Some patients continue to develop coronary heart disease despite successful treatment, suggesting that other particles transporting fats through the bloodstream play an important role. Until recently, the biological reasons behind this remaining risk were not well understood.

"For this study, we wanted to understand what happens beyond the accumulation of cholesterol in artery walls, whether different fat-carrying particles can damage the blood vessels differently and why the remaining risk of heart disease still occurs," says Jakub Morze, lead author and a postdoctoral fellow at Chalmers University of Technology, in Sweden.

Cholesterol is a substance similar to fat that circulates in the bloodstream. The body needs it to build cells and manufacture certain vitamins and hormones. Problems can arise when too much cholesterol accumulates in blood vessel walls, creating deposits called plaques.

These plaques can narrow arteries and interfere with blood flow. If a plaque ruptures, a blood clot may form quickly and completely obstruct the affected vessel, potentially triggering a heart attack or stroke.

Because cholesterol and other fats cannot travel through the blood on their own, they are transported by specialized particles known as lipoproteins. Three major classes of these particles contain a surface protein called apolipoprotein B (apoB). When too many of these particles circulate in the blood, they can deliver excess cholesterol into artery walls. The cholesterol they carry is commonly referred to as "bad cholesterol."

To investigate these unanswered questions, the scientists used proteomics analysis to examine how three types of fat-carrying particles (LDL, TRL and Lp(a)) affect the body and may contribute to heart disease. This approach allowed the team to investigate biological changes associated with the particles rather than focusing exclusively on the cholesterol they carry.

All three types can contribute to cholesterol deposits inside artery walls, although LDL, which stands for low-density lipoprotein, is the most common. In a previous study, the same research group found that counting harmful lipoprotein particles was the most effective way to predict future heart disease risk.

The researchers also identified two particularly important contributors beyond LDL: triglyceride-rich lipoproteins, or TRL, and lipoprotein(a), known as Lp(a). Their earlier findings suggested that each of these particles poses a greater risk individually than an LDL particle. As a result, TRL and Lp(a) are considered major contributors to the cardiovascular danger that can persist even after LDL cholesterol has been successfully reduced.

Proteomics is the systematic, large-scale examination and measurement of proteins within cells, tissues, or body fluids at a particular point in time.

While genomics investigates a person's relatively stable DNA, proteomics focuses on proteins, which are constantly responding to changes inside the body. These molecules help construct tissues, process food, transmit hormonal messages, and defend against infections.

Because protein patterns shift in response to factors such as diet, stress, aging, and disease, analyzing them can provide a snapshot of current biological activity. Proteomics can help researchers identify biomarkers, diagnose medical conditions, and track how patients respond to treatment.

Blood Proteins Reveal Hidden Heart Disease Risks

The new investigation focused on proteins, which perform countless essential functions throughout the body. Unlike genetic information, which remains largely unchanged, protein levels and activity can respond to diet, stress, aging, and illness. Studying these changes can therefore provide valuable insights into the body's current biological condition.

Researchers analyzed measurements of nearly 3,000 proteins found in blood samples and compared the results with genetic information and long-term health records. This combination helped them identify protein patterns associated with different lipoprotein particles and provided clues about how those particles might contribute to damage inside the arteries.

One of the most striking discoveries involved TRL and Lp(a). Although these are distinct types of particles, their associated blood protein patterns showed substantial similarities. Those overlapping patterns also appeared to be linked to the later development of heart disease.

The researchers found that these particles carried proteins capable of attracting immune cells, potentially encouraging inflammation and changes in the structure of blood vessel walls. This suggests that TRL and Lp(a) may contribute to cardiovascular disease through some of the same biological processes, rather than simply depositing cholesterol in the arteries.

LDL showed a different pattern. Its associated proteins were primarily connected to cholesterol accumulation in artery walls, highlighting an important distinction between the ways these three types of particles may contribute to heart disease.

"The overlap for TRL and Lp(a) is one of the most interesting findings," says Morze. "It suggests that these particles may affect some of the same inflammatory and vascular processes. This could help identify targets for more precisely directed prevention in the future."

How LDL, TRL, and Lp(a) Affect Heart Health

The three types of lipoproteins examined in the study, LDL, TRL, and Lp(a), transport different amounts of cholesterol and other fats through the bloodstream. Each contains the structural protein apolipoprotein B, or apoB.

All three can contribute to atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty material accumulates inside blood vessel walls. As these deposits develop, they increase the risk of coronary heart disease.

LDL: Low-density lipoprotein transports most of the cholesterol circulating in the blood. An LDL cholesterol measurement indicates how much cholesterol is contained within these particles.

TRL: Triglyceride-rich lipoproteins transport cholesterol along with triglycerides, which the body uses as an important energy source. As triglycerides are removed from these particles, the remaining fragments can deposit cholesterol inside artery walls. In this study, the TRL measurements primarily reflected liver-produced particles called VLDL and the remnants they leave behind.

Lp(a): Lipoprotein(a) resembles an LDL particle but contains an additional protein known as apolipoprotein(a). Higher levels of Lp(a) are already recognized as an established risk factor for coronary heart disease.

Could the Discovery Lead to Better Heart Disease Prevention?

By identifying biological pathways associated with cardiovascular risk beyond LDL cholesterol, the findings offer researchers new possibilities for developing more personalized prevention strategies. In particular, the shared inflammatory and blood vessel effects linked to TRL and Lp(a) could become promising areas for further investigation.

However, the research did not evaluate a new treatment or establish a blood protein test ready for routine clinical use. Additional studies will be needed to determine whether measuring these biological processes, or developing treatments that target them, can improve protection against heart disease.

"Lowering LDL cholesterol remains a cornerstone of prevention," says Clemens Wittenbecher, who led the study and is Assistant Professor of Precision Medicine and Diagnostics at Chalmers. "Our findings point to biological processes that may help explain some of the risk that remains beyond LDL. The next step is to establish whether measuring or targeting these processes can improve prevention alongside existing treatments."

The results reinforce the importance of controlling LDL cholesterol while revealing why cholesterol reduction alone may not address every source of cardiovascular risk. Understanding the additional ways blood particles affect arteries could ultimately help scientists develop more precise approaches to protecting heart health.

The study, "Apolipoprotein B-containing lipoproteins: distinct roles in atherosclerosis revealed by plasma proteomic profiling," was published in the European Heart Journal.

The research authors are Jakub Morze, Elias Björnson, Michael Y Mi, Martin Adiels, Giorgio E Melloni, Gonçalo Rosas da Silva, Andrzej Rynkiewicz, Nicholas A Marston, Marta Guasch-Ferré, Michael Y Tsai, Jerome I Rotter, Robert E Gerszten, Qi Sun, Frank B Hu, Rikard Landberg, Göran Bergström, Chris J Packard, Jan Borén and Clemens Wittenbecher.

At the time of the research, the authors were affiliated with Chalmers University of Technology and the Institute of Medicine at the University of Gothenburg, Sweden; Harvard Medical School, USA; AstraZeneca, Sweden; Municipal Hospital in Olsztyn, Poland; University of Copenhagen, Denmark; University of Minnesota, USA; The Lundquist Institute at Harbour-UCLA Medical Center in Torrance, USA; Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, USA; and the University of Glasgow, UK.
