#5708. Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't

A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed. Now, scientists at Yale have taken an important step toward identifying which treatments can actually influence biological aging and which ones show little measurable benefit.

Their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests. Popular over-the-counter supplements examined in the research, however, showed little evidence of producing the same effects.

The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.

From Fighting Cancer to Understanding Aging

When Raghav Sehgal began graduate school at Yale several years ago, he planned to use advanced computer science techniques to investigate cancer. His background in engineering and experience launching a computational biology startup had given him a strong foundation for that work.

However, a question from his Ph.D. adviser at the Yale School of Medicine changed his research direction. Rather than focusing on individual diseases such as cancer or cardiovascular disease, why not investigate the aging process that contributes to their development?

"That put me on a different path," said Sehgal, now an associate research scientist in psychiatry who specializes in computational biology and bioinformatics. "As researchers, we have a long way to go in understanding the aging process and whether the steps we take to manage it really work."

Sehgal now studies the biological mechanisms behind human aging, how scientists can measure those changes, and why getting older increases the likelihood of conditions such as cancer, diabetes, and dementia. His work also explores whether interventions might reverse certain aspects of biological aging, even if eliminating aging itself remains beyond reach.

New DNA Tests Reveal Which Anti-Aging Treatments Work

Sehgal is the lead author of the new study, which was conducted in the laboratory of Albert Higgins-Chen, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine. The research team set out to determine which existing approaches to slowing aging produce changes that can be reliably measured.

Their analysis found encouraging results for certain medications and lifestyle interventions. In contrast, the over-the-counter supplements included in the study generally failed to produce meaningful reductions in biological age.

The project involved the entire Higgins-Chen laboratory, including Daniel Borrus, Jenel F. Armstrong, John Gonzalez, Jessica Kasamoto, and Yaroslav Markov.

"For the first time we've shown that certain therapies have measurable impacts," said Sehgal. "This wasn't previously possible, because we didn't have enough data to say these biomarkers are consistently responsive to these interventions."

Biomarkers provide measurable information about what is happening inside the body. In aging research, they can help estimate a person's biological or functional age, which may differ from their chronological age.

To investigate whether treatments could influence aging, the Yale team relied primarily on blood-based measurements called epigenetic clocks.

These tools analyze chemical patterns attached to DNA, particularly methyl groups (basic chemical structures that act like tags). Previous research has shown that these chemical markers change as people grow older. Some interventions may reverse certain age-associated patterns, and computer algorithms use those changes to estimate a person's biological age.

The researchers brought together findings from 51 clinical studies investigating different anti-aging strategies. These ranged from dietary supplements and medications to lifestyle changes and medical procedures.

Across those studies, the team examined more than 110 DNA methylation biomarkers (including 16 major epigenetic clocks). By comparing measurements taken before and after interventions, they could evaluate which approaches were associated with reductions in biological age.

"What we did was pretty unique," Sehgal said. "We already know that certain things might prolong health span and lifespan. There is data from retrospective analysis as well as from animal models. We took all that knowledge along with the real-world clinical studies to identify which interventions in humans were slowing down aging across the board in these known biomarkers."

Which Anti-Aging Treatments Showed the Best Results?

The researchers divided the interventions into four main groups: prescription drugs, lifestyle modifications, over-the-counter supplements, and medical procedures.

One of the clearest findings involved diet and exercise. Combining regular physical activity with a healthy eating plan consistently reduced epigenetic age. The dietary approaches examined included Mediterranean, low-fat, and low-carb diets.

The strongest reductions in biological age markers were associated with certain pharmaceutical treatments. These included metformin and semaglutide, prescription medications used to manage metabolic conditions and body weight, as well as anti-TNF therapies that target a protein involved in the body's inflammatory response.

(TNF, or tumor necrosis factor, is an immune-system protein that helps fight inflammation-related injury.)

The findings were less encouraging for over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures. In the studies examined, these approaches did not produce measurable reductions in epigenetic age.

The researchers also discovered that newer biological age clocks performed better than older versions. Another important finding was that people living with diseases generally experienced larger changes in their aging biomarkers than healthy participants.

Could DNA Blood Tests Transform Anti-Aging Research?

According to Sehgal, the next priority is to test these findings in larger, more diverse populations. This would help researchers determine how consistently different treatments influence biological aging across people with different health conditions and backgrounds.

The improved blood tests could also dramatically shorten the time needed to evaluate potential anti-aging therapies.

"If these new biomarkers are eventually validated to predict long-term health, scientists will be able to evaluate anti-aging therapies much faster," he added. "Instead of waiting decades for evidence from clinical trials, we'll be able to see which interventions are effective and in which people in a few years or even months."

That possibility could represent a major advance for aging research. Instead of relying entirely on clinical studies that follow participants for decades, scientists might eventually use validated biological age measurements to identify promising treatments much earlier.

However, senior author Higgins-Chen stressed that scientists must be careful about interpreting what changes in aging biomarkers actually mean.

"We have developed a rigorous, systematic approach to evaluating and comparing how biomarkers change across a wide variety of interventions, and that is a critical step in the right direction," he said. "However, the true meaning of that change must be fully understood."

Important Questions About Slowing Aging Remain

Although the results are promising, several major questions remain unanswered.

For example, researchers still need to establish whether changes in biological age are directly caused by a treatment or influenced by other factors that were not accounted for. They also need to understand how quickly those changes occur, whether they persist after treatment ends, and which biological processes produce them.

Most importantly, scientists have not yet established whether lowering epigenetic age leads to meaningful improvements in long-term health.

"And most importantly - what does the change mean for our long-term risk of age-related disease and functional decline?" Higgins-Chen said.

Further investigations into these questions are underway, with additional studies led by Borrus, Armstrong, and Grace Zou.

The Higgins-Chen laboratory is also affiliated with Yale's Department of Pathology, the Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Program, and the Y-Age Yale Center for Research on Aging.

What Appears to Work Against Biological Aging?

Based on the improved DNA-based blood tests, the Yale researchers identified two particularly promising approaches for reducing biological age markers:

The analysis also identified benefits from certain anti-TNF medications, while the tested over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures showed little measurable effect.

These results provide a clearer picture of which interventions may influence biological aging. However, more research is needed to confirm the findings and determine whether reductions in biological age markers ultimately translate into fewer age-related diseases, better health, or longer lives.

#5707. Hitachi Vantara bets smarter storage can close AI’s pilot-to-production gap

Enterprises pushing AI from pilot to production are learning that data, not GPUs, is the hardest part, and open table formats such as Apache Iceberg are part of the answer. Demand for AI infrastructure shows few signs of slowing, but much of the information companies need is still scattered, ungoverned and out of reach.

That pressure is turning storage into an active layer that classifies, governs and serves data to models. Unstructured files such as logs and medical images hold intelligence AI can now extract, according to Arun Prasad Raman (pictured, left), vice president of hybrid cloud and AI infrastructure at Hitachi Vantara Corp.

“Storage is not seen as just storing the data,” Raman said. “You need to bring in more intelligence natively rather than moving the data to another replication and bringing it back for, say, indexing. If it can do it natively, that’s where the value add is.”

Raman and Jeff Lundberg (right), principal product and solutions manager at Hitachi Vantara, spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Gemma Allen at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed AI’s pilot-to-production gap, Apache Iceberg and how Hitachi Vantara is adding intelligence to storage. (* Disclosure below.)

Reference architectures for AI factories and data platforms are largely settled. Most projects stall because data is spread across on-premises systems, software-as-a-service applications and the cloud, while access control, governance and shifting regulations add friction, according to Lundberg. Hitachi Vantara is responding with industry-specific solutions built on its Hitachi iQ stack and its sister businesses’ rail and energy experience, he explained.

“It’s about the outcome more so than the technology that we’re trying to put into place,” Lundberg said. “That’s an enabler to get you to the solution you’re trying to get to.”

Much of that work now happens in storage. Last week, Hitachi Vantara expanded its VSP One platform with new object storage and data lakehouse capabilities. A service in its object store flags files containing personal information, such as Social Security numbers. Data scientists can then keep that data out of specific models or block its replication to another country, Raman explained.

“That’s the intelligence we are adding into the storage itself,” Raman said. “So that’s where the evolution of storage is making it more intelligent.”

Analytics follow the same logic. CT scan metadata can be stored in Apache Iceberg format on the company’s object store and queried directly. An application could list every abdominal scan from the past year without a separate extract, transform and load or ETL process or database, Raman noted.

“Whether it’s a backup or it’s 10 years old, it still carries some intelligence,” Raman said. “As long as it carries intelligence, it becomes important to AI.”

#5706. AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death

More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss

The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.

The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict

Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening

Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."

Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."

Materials provided by University of California - Berkeley. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5705. A 19-year study reveals a troubling link between napping and death

A daily nap may seem like a harmless way to recharge, but new research suggests that certain napping habits could provide important clues about a person's health as they age. Scientists have found that taking longer or more frequent naps, particularly in the morning, is associated with an increased risk of death among older adults.

Researchers from Mass General Brigham and Rush University Medical Center examined the napping patterns of 1,338 older adults over a period of up to 19 years. Their findings, published in JAMA Network Open, suggest that monitoring daytime sleep could help identify underlying medical conditions or early signs of declining health.

"Excessive napping later in life has been linked to neurodegeneration, cardiovascular diseases and even greater morbidity, but many of those findings rely on self-reported napping habits and leave out metrics like when and how regular those naps are," said lead author Chenlu Gao, PhD, an investigator in the Department of Anesthesiology at Mass General Brigham and an affiliated research fellow in the Division of Sleep and Circadian Disorders in the Department of Medicine. "Our study is one of the first to show an association between objectively measured nap patterns and mortality and suggests there is immense clinical value in tracking napping patterns to catch health conditions early."

Why Scientists Are Studying Daytime Napping

Daytime naps are common among older adults, with estimates suggesting that 20% to 60% regularly nap. An occasional nap can help restore energy and improve alertness, but excessive daytime sleeping in later life has been associated with several health concerns.

Despite these connections, researchers still have an incomplete understanding of how specific napping behaviors relate to long-term health. Many earlier studies depended on participants remembering and reporting their own sleep habits, which may not provide an accurate picture. They also often overlooked important details, such as how long naps lasted, when they occurred, and how much napping patterns changed from one day to the next.

To obtain more reliable measurements, the research team analyzed information from the Rush Memory and Aging Project. Launched in 1997, this long-running study was designed primarily to investigate memory, thinking abilities, and neurological decline among older adults in northern Illinois, most of whom were white.

Starting in 2005, participants wore wrist activity monitors for 10 days to record their daily periods of rest and movement. Researchers used these measurements to identify daytime sleep and assess nap duration, frequency, timing, and daily variation.

Longer and More Frequent Naps Linked to Higher Mortality Risk

By 2025, researchers had assembled up to 19 years of follow-up information from 1,338 participants. They then examined whether napping habits measured during the initial assessment were associated with the likelihood of dying from any cause during the subsequent years.

The results revealed several notable patterns. Older adults who slept longer during the day or took naps more frequently had higher mortality rates. The timing of naps also appeared to matter.

Each additional hour spent napping per day was associated with approximately a 13% higher mortality risk. Taking one additional nap per day was linked to about a 7% increase in risk.

One of the most striking findings involved morning naps. Participants who napped in the morning had a 30% higher mortality risk compared with those who napped in the afternoon.

However, not every aspect of napping was associated with poorer outcomes. Researchers found no increased mortality risk linked to irregular napping schedules, suggesting that changes in nap timing or duration from day to day were not necessarily indicators of greater risk.

Could Napping Habits Reveal Hidden Health Problems?

The researchers emphasize that their findings do not mean daytime naps directly cause health problems or shorten lives. Instead, excessive napping may reflect medical conditions or changes in the body that have not yet been recognized.

"It is important to note that this is correlation, not causation. Excessive napping is likely indicating underlying disease, chronic conditions, sleep disturbances, or circadian dysregulation," said Gao. "Now that we know there is a strong correlation between napping patterns and mortality rates, we can make the case to implement wearable daytime nap assessments to predict health conditions and prevent further decline."

These findings raise the possibility that wearable activity trackers could eventually become useful tools for monitoring health in older adults. By identifying changes in daytime sleep habits, healthcare professionals might be able to recognize warning signs of underlying illness, disrupted sleep cycles, or neurological decline earlier.

Although further research is needed to determine how effectively napping patterns can predict specific medical conditions, the study suggests that something as ordinary as a daily nap could provide valuable information about a person's overall health.

Study Authorship, Disclosures, and Funding

Authorship: In addition to Gao and Li, the Mass General Brigham researchers involved in the study include Ruixue Cai, Xi Zheng, Arlen Gaba, Lei Gao, and Kun Hu. Other contributors include Lei Yu, Aron S. Buchman, and David A. Bennett.

Disclosures: Li received a financial gift from iFutureLab to support research and has received consulting payments for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Cardiac Dynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Li also received an honorarium for delivering a lecture at Shandong University.

Hu has received consulting fees for serving on the iFutureLab-HEKA Scientific Advisory Board as Chair of Medical Biodynamics and Honorary Life-Time Co-Founder. Mass General Brigham reviewed and managed the interests of both Li and Hu under its conflict of interest policies. These interests are unrelated to the present research.

Funding: The research received support from the American Academy of Sleep Medicine Foundation (290-FP-22), the Alzheimer's Association Research Fellowship to Promote Diversity (AARFD-22-928372), and the National Institute on Aging (RF1AG064312; R01AG083799).

Gao C. received additional funding from the National Heart Lung and Blood Institute (5T32HL007901). Li received support from the BrightFocus Foundation (A2020886S) and startup funding from the Department of Anesthesia, Critical Care and Pain Medicine at Massachusetts General Hospital. Hu also received startup funding from the same department.

Gao L. received additional support from the Alzheimer's Association (AACSF-23-1148490), National Institute on Aging (R03AG087439), American Academy of Sleep Medicine (352-DS-24), and National Institute of General Medical Sciences (R35GM160254).

The Rush Memory and Aging Project was funded by the National Institutes of Health (R01AG056352 and R01AG017917).

#5704. Ella Langley Makes CMA Awards History—Inside the Home Where She’ll Put Her New Trophies on Display

Singer Ella Langley made history at the Country Music Awards when she set the record for the most CMA awards won by a woman in one night—so will where the hitmaker house her new trophies?

The "Choosin Texas" singer, 27, won entertainer of the year, female vocalist of the year, album of the year, single of the year, and song of the year.

When accepting her sixth award of the evening, she teased, "At this point, I'm sick of me!"

“This has been the most special night. I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life," she added.

At one point during the evening, fellow country star Lainey Wilson joked, "I said I was gonna bring you a bedazzled broom. I knew you was gonna sweep, girl.”

At the end of the evening, Langley posed with all of her awards as she smiled from ear to ear.

Langley will put her multiple trophies on display at her lakefront retreat, which she picked up in 2025.

In July 2025, Langley snapped up her first-ever home in her hometown of Montgomery, AL, just minutes away from her parents' home.

Langley, who lives in Nashville, TN, but was born and raised in Alabama, gushed about her newly minted purchase while speaking to Audacy, telling the radio station that she decided to make her first real estate investment in her home state because she feels most like herself when she's there.

"It just brings me back to who I am at the root of me every time I go back there. And when it comes to writing songs and being in that state of mind, I think it’s important to have a place like that," she said.

The star noted that, while she will likely "always" live in Tennessee, which is the home of country music, she will continue to keep roots in Alabama because of how close she is to her family.

“I think I’ll always have to live in Tennessee to some extent in my life, but being from Alabama, it’s so close. It’s under four hours to get there," she added.

Though many young people might find the process of buying their first property overwhelming, Langley conceded that she was in a much more privileged position—namely because she has her own business managers who helped to oversee the entire purchase.

"I honestly been having a blast. I have great business management. They just get all the phone calls, yes or no, this is what I want to do, and they figure out all the little logistics, so very thankful for them,” she added.

Langley moved to Nashville in order to pursue her musical career, relocating from her hometown in Alabama in 2019.

"The music family here is just really special; people are so willing to be a mentor or help you grow in a way I just couldn’t do back home," Langley said of her new home state during an interview with Raised Rowdy.

Previously, Langley has shared that her move to Nashville also helped her to find more freedom in her writing process, joking to Raised Rowdy that she spent much of her childhood in Alabama trying to "survive life" with two brothers.

"I grew up in the country in Alabama between two brothers, so a lot of my childhood was just trying to survive life between those two," she said.

"I always was trying to prove I was just as tough and fearless as they were. Being a tomboy like that, a lot of my friends ended up being guys. If you ask my band or people who know me, they’ll tell you sometimes I seem more like a guy than a girl. But I think women can still be direct, strong, and tough, without apologizing for who they are or how they think."

Making the decision to pursue her music full time was a serious one for Langley, who dropped out of Auburn University in order to focus on her passion.

“I had a boyfriend who was in music and then his manager, they were both moving to Nashville and we’re going to live with Trey (Lewis). And I was like, well hell, I’m not staying here," she previously told CountryNow.

"So I called mom and dad and I said, ‘Hey, I think I want to drop out of school and move to Nashville. I’m just going to be in more debt anyways when I graduate. I mean, I’m going to go do this anyways. I would rather start it now.'"

The singer also revealed that she was warmly welcomed to Nashville.

“It’s been a cool journey of finding those people for me in town that I just love and love me and believe in me and I believe in them. And so that’s what’s really kept me going a lot through this," she went on.

"And obviously my family supports me the way that they do and just love me, but that’s the thing, nobody has ever thought I was going to do anything else …

"If you ask any of my family, they’re like, ‘Yeah, we all knew that this was what she was going to do.’ So there wasn’t ever really any question when I wanted to move."

#5703. Vitalik Buterin Wants Crypto to Have Housing’s Stability, But Can Ethereum Deliver?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Ethereum co-founder Vitalik Buterin believes younger generations investing in stocks and digital assets instead of housing could help ease pressure on property prices. However, he says crypto still needs something that makes housing attractive: stability.

Buterin thinks that housing creates incentives for owners to keep property prices high, even when cheaper homes would benefit society. Digital assets could offer an alternative, but today’s platforms often encourage excessive speculation.

“We need the equivalent of those good properties that housing investment has, for modern digital assets,” Buterin wrote on X

His comments raise a question for Ethereum. Can the network evolve beyond speculative trading and become dependable infrastructure for people building long-term digital wealth?

One benefit of younger generations investing more in stonks and other digital things instead of housing is that it reduces perverse incentives that drive people to push to keep housing expensive, instead of rejoicing when prices drop as we do for all other life necessities.That…

Ethereum’s development roadmap increasingly focuses on making the network faster, more efficient, and harder to disrupt. Its next major upgrade, Glamsterdam, is in testing, and ethereum.org lists a mainnet launch for Q4 2026 with no date confirmed yet. The upgrade introduces several changes designed to improve Ethereum’s capacity without sacrificing decentralization.

One major feature is Enshrined Proposer-Builder Separation (ePBS). It moves the relationship between block proposers and builders directly into Ethereum’s protocol, reducing reliance on external relays and additional trust assumptions.

Another important development is Block-Level Access Lists. The feature prepares Ethereum to process unrelated transactions in parallel rather than handling everything sequentially.

These improvements could help Ethereum support more financial applications while keeping its infrastructure accessible to independent node operators. So, if digital assets are expected to become long-term financial instruments rather than vehicles for short-term speculation, this is very much needed.

Ethereum also provides an established foundation for staking, stablecoins, decentralized lending, and tokenized real-world assets. These applications could give investors more ways to hold and use digital wealth without constantly trading volatile tokens.

Yet, security, reliable applications, and responsible financial products must develop alongside network capacity.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Ethereum’s market performance presents a contrasting picture. ETH is trading just a notch above $1,800. This leaves the coin 63% below its all-time high of $4,946. The decline highlights the gap between Ethereum’s technological ambitions and its current market valuation.

Ethereum’s network utility and ETH’s investment performance are also not interchangeable. More applications and transactions can strengthen the ecosystem, but they do not create proportional demand for ETH.

The token still plays an important role as Ethereum’s native transaction currency, staking asset, and collateral across decentralized finance. For this reason, continued growth in staking, stablecoins, and tokenized assets could strengthen ETH’s underlying investment narrative.

Buterin’s comments are bigger than a debate about housing affordability. He is effectively challenging the crypto industry to build assets and platforms that encourage long-term ownership rather than constant speculation.

Ethereum has several pieces of that foundation already, including proof-of-stake security, smart contracts, and an expanding financial ecosystem.

Its upcoming upgrades aim to improve the infrastructure supporting those applications. But the network still needs to prove that its technology can deliver dependable financial products at scale.

#5702. 5 Packing Tips for a Smooth Move

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

Greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert says, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need."

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

#5701. D-Matrix bets stacked DRAM can solve inference’s memory bandwidth problem

As artificial intelligence workloads shift to inference, memory bandwidth decides whether hardware generates tokens quickly or sits idle. D-Matrix Corp. is answering with Raptor, a second-generation chip stacking 3D DRAM beneath its compute logic.

AI infrastructure has become a systems game, and winners combine memory, interconnect and software into cohesive designs, according to Satyam Srivastava (pictured), fellow at d-Matrix.

“It’s no longer a chip problem. Chip plays a part of it. Memory bandwidth is a fundamental advantage that has to be solved,” Srivastava said. “The next is energy efficiency. The next is interconnect efficiency. The next is software cohesiveness.”

Srivastava spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed d-Matrix’s Raptor chip and its stacked 3D DRAM, inference memory bandwidth and the shift toward heterogeneous computing. (* Disclosure below.)

D-Matrix proves each risky technology on a test chip first. Jayhawk proved die-to-die connectivity, and Jayhawk II validated digital in-memory computing. The Corsair accelerator combined both and entered full production earlier this year, Srivastava explained.

“Fast forward, we have the Pavehawk chip, test chip, which is proving out 3D DRAM stacked underneath the logic die, which serves as the core technology for Raptor, which is our second-generation chip coming out next year,” Srivastava said.

Stacking keeps the distributed memory architecture intact but moves memory cells onto a separate layer rather than consuming logic die area. Data travels a short distance and never crosses an interposer. That puts 3D DRAM in a new tier between SRAM and high-bandwidth memory, Srivastava said.

“So you’re getting 10 times higher energy efficiency compared to HBM, 10 times higher bandwidth compared to HBM, where it sits in between SRAM and HBM in terms of capacity,” Srivastava said.

Pairing a Corsair-based server with an existing Hopper GPU fleet can raise utilization from about 20% to as much as 80%, meaning more tokens per dollar, Srivastava noted. D-Matrix has also adopted NVLink Fusion rackscale infrastructure from Nvidia Corp. to connect its accelerators to Nvidia’s AI factories.

“For us, it unlocks the opportunity to participate in a very established ecosystem, the world’s most popular AI factory. We get access to a very hardened design of an MGX rack,” Srivastava said.

The partnership points toward heterogeneous computing, where software orchestrates GPUs, CPUs and accelerators such as Raptor as one system, with the cluster as the unit of computing, Srivastava explained.

“So think of a chip, but that chip is an entire cluster and it has many different hardware units,” Srivastava said. “Some are GPUs, some are CPUs, some are ASIC accelerators, and you can use whichever one you like to serve the needs of the workload the best.”

#5700. Mastering Digital Marketing - How to Grow Your Business Online

Having a solid digital marketing strategy is essential if you want to succeed as a business owner in the modern day. Effective digital marketing lets you get more eyes on your business and ensure consistent growth.

Because digital marketing trends are forever changing, it’s important to stay on top of your brand’s strategy. Doing so ensures that you stand out above your competitors and gain the recognition that your brand deserves.

If you’re unsure how to master your digital marketing strategy, consider working with an expert company that can help you figure out which direction to go. A professional agency, such as Scorpion Digital Marketing Agency, can support your online efforts to maximize your success.

If you don’t want to outsource your digital marketing processes, try these top tips below to maintain an effective digital marketing strategy and boost your business growth.

Your website is where most of your new audience will find your business and your existing customers will shop for your new products and services. If you create a strong first impression through your website, you can gain credibility and authority in your industry.

Make sure to regularly update your website content so it’s accurate and on-trend. Doing so also signals to Google that your website is authoritative and credible, increasing your rankings on search engine results pages (SERPs).

The higher your rankings, the higher your visibility, meaning you can expand your reach with minimal effort. When updating your content, use plenty of industry-relevant keywords and key phrases to ensure your target audience finds your site.

#5699. Thanksgiving Costs at Home Jump 6% in 2026 as Grocery and Utility Bills Hit Hosts Hard

Thanksgiving is the perfect time for loved ones to gather over a delicious, hearty meal. But in 2026, that feast could come with a higher price tag than we’d like.

According to the American Farm Bureau, the average cost of a 10-person holiday dinner will rise by 6% from 2025 to $5.86 per person. That’s because staples like turkey, milk, rolls, and cranberries have shot up in price.

And unfortunately, the higher price tag doesn’t stop at the grocery store. You may also notice a spike in your utility bills as your home’s systems are forced to work harder to keep everyone comfortable.

The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) found that the average family already uses over 300 gallons of water per day at home. With increased usage from additional showers, dishwashing, and hand-washing that are typical during the holidays, costs are sure to climb.

“Having guests over greatly drives up money spent on groceries, but it also drives up utility costs. Preparing all of that food often involves keeping ovens and burners running for multiple hours and using large amounts of water in both the cooking and cleaning processes,” explains Carrie Barnard, founder and recipe developer at Eating on a Dime.

Fortunately, it’s still possible to enjoy Thanksgiving without breaking the bank. A bit of planning and creativity can help keep your grocery expenses and utility bill in check.

Where you live can also impact how much you spend this Thanksgiving.

The American Farm Bureau found that the 10-person classic dinner in the Northeast is about 5% higher than the national average of $61.57.

Costs in the West ($58.74) and Midwest ($56.89) are closer to the national average. And if you live in the South, you could expect to pay around $54.33.

There are a few reasons for these cost differences.

“They largely have to do with supply chains, since different regions require different imports, and these imprints cost more the further they travel,” says Barnard.

Since the Northeast is generally colder, it relies more heavily on imports for many Thanksgiving staples, which leads to a higher cost for consumers. Also, the Northeast typically has higher operating costs for businesses, meaning that grocery prices are often higher.

“However, prices vary widely between different stores, and many of them offer special holiday promotions, so there are usually savings to be found,” Barnard adds.

While grocery and energy costs may be higher this Thanksgiving, these tips can help reduce them and enjoy the holiday without overspending.

Jim Wang, founder at Wallet Hacks in Fulton, MD, suggests exploring promotions at your local supermarkets and groceries.

“Many stores know consumers are being squeezed and often try to put out promos around Thanksgiving. They may offer the turkey at a low cost to get you to make your entire holiday purchase there,” Wang explains.

Depending on how you celebrate Thanksgiving and who attends your meal, a potluck might make sense.

“Every year, we do a potluck with friends and everyone brings something to share. This defrays the costs across everyone and while you don't end up with nearly as many leftovers, that's also excess spending you can avoid, especially if Thanksgiving leftovers don't excite you,” says Wang.

If you’re hosting, be a bit more conservative about how much everyone will eat.

“Sometimes we get concerned about having guests leave hungry and we make too much as a result,” Wang says.

It’s perfectly OK to make less of the more expensive items, like proteins, and bigger portions of sides that they can fill up on. Chances are your guests may prefer those sides to the turkey anyway.

Barnard tries to use her air fryer and slow cooker rather than my full oven when possible.

“These appliances are highly versatile and able to cook a wide variety of dishes, and they consume much less energy in the process,” explains Barnard.

Unlike ovens, which leak out heat and consume more energy the more you open the door to check on your food, air fryers and slow cookers cook things quickly and efficiently with low energy.

“I try to only use the oven when it’s required due to the size or amount of food involved,” Barnard adds.

#5698. AI inference servers shrink to fit the air-cooled racks enterprises already run

Power-efficient inference chips are becoming the entry price for enterprises that want to run AI on hardware they own.

As AI shifts from building models to running them every day, costly graphics processing unit racks and the liquid cooling they demand keep many companies renting compute instead. That gap is opening room for challengers to the incumbent chipmakers. Axelera AI B.V. built its business at the edge with low-power chips and edge AI development tools, and it is now taking that technology into data center infrastructure, according to Manuel Botija (pictured), vice president and head of product at Axelera.

“Enterprises cannot own their own infrastructure. They’re locked out because of the cost and the power,” Botija said. “We are enabling them now to own it. It’s not that we are helping the world save power or save money — which we are — but it’s that we are unlocking use cases that were simply not possible before.”

Botija spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at SC26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how power-efficient inference chips are heading for the data center and how enterprises locked out by the cost and power of GPU racks can own their own AI infrastructure instead of renting compute. (* Disclosure below.)

Axelera’s Europa chip has been shipping since September. Ahead of SC26, the company unveiled Titania, a third-generation architecture that scales the design up to a 400-watt chip. The resulting six-kilowatt server is built to perform like leading data center GPUs while fitting into the existing 20- to 30-kilowatt air-cooled racks of an ordinary enterprise data center, Botija explained.

“Having a six-kilowatt server that can perform like a data centre GPU is a pretty big deal,” he said. “It basically means that they have some storage equipment, some networking equipment, some traditional CPU equipment, and next to all of that, they can also insert some AI inference hardware acceleration without needing to go and rebuild another server room or another data center.”

For enterprises that would rather own their AI hardware than pay a recurring cloud bill, the barriers have been steep. A GPU rack costs at least $1 million, often far more, and usually requires liquid cooling, Botija noted. Axelera’s answer rests on digital in-memory computing, a technique that grew out of its founders’ research and gives the company’s power-efficient inference chips a performance-per-watt advantage.

“Now you can own your own infrastructure,” Botija said. “You can amortize those investments and … reduce your opex, and therefore be more profitable as a company.”

#5697. Chris Simms Scores a $4.5 Million NYC Home—Weeks After Selling His Longtime Connecticut Retreat

Former Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Chris Simms has picked up a $4.5 million New York City residence—after offloading his longtime Connecticut estate for $5.5 million.

The 45-year-old—who retired from the NFL in 2010 following a spleen injury—and his wife, Daniella, recently picked up the property, which is located in Sutton Tower.

His new pad comes complete with three bedrooms, 3.5 bathrooms, and floor-to-ceiling windows, according to the New York Post, who first reported the sale. The property also boasts a chef's kitchen and panoramic views.

The Sutton Place tower was built in 2022 by architect Thomas Juul-Hansen. The residence is known to be the tallest tower on the East Side.

As a member of the luxe dwelling, Simms and his wife get access to a resort-style pool, a gym, a personal training studio, saunas, and a spa space.

His purchase came weeks after Realtor.com® exclusively revealed that he sold his Connecticut property for $5.5 million.

He initially put their longtime Greenwich abode on the market on Feb. 6. Within a matter of months, they had dropped the price by $500,000.

A second price cut in June slashed a further $600,000 from the ask, while a third discount on Aug. 21 saw the athlete's original ask of $8 million lowered to $6.2 million, a move that ultimately bagged a buyer for Simms' dwelling.

Simms, who now serves as an analyst for NBC Sports, purchased the home for $2.5 million in 2019—shortly after he and his wife invested heavily in its restoration and renovation.

The property, which was originally built in 1725, has been updated extensively in the seven years since the couple took ownership.

Today, the property is hailed as a "piece of Greenwich history" with all the luxury of a modern mansion.

"A fully restored antique farmhouse offering approximately 3,669 square feet of refined living space, set on extraordinary level acreage with sweeping meadow views and an irreplaceable country setting across from protected conservation land with direct access to the Greenwich Riding Trails," the listing, which was held by Monica Webster of Douglas Elliman, noted.

The five-bedroom, five-bathroom dwelling features an open floor plan that begins with a living area with a cozy fireplace, windows, and wooden beams on the ceiling.

The chef's kitchen boasts state-of-the-art appliances, a white marble island, and white cabinetry.

The charming dining area also has wooden beams on the ceiling and a wooden island.

The bedrooms follow the home's minimalistic aesthetic and feature enough space for a queen-sized bed while boasting small windows.

"The residence blends historic authenticity with modern luxury, featuring wide-plank antique floors, exposed beams, preserved fireplaces, and original architectural details," the listing added.

The bathrooms feature double vanities, a large glass-enclosed shower, a marble soaking tub, and sliding barn doors.

Elsewhere, there is a gym, spa center with a massage chair, and an outdoor entertaining area with a foosball table.

Throughout the home, modern aesthetics have been meticulously merged with historic charm.

"A thoughtful renovation delivers elevated comfort throughout, including a newly created primary suite with cathedral ceilings, floor-to-ceiling windows, a bespoke dressing room, and a private staircase to a serene, light-filled office and library retreat for everyday living," the listing stated.

Simms and his wife lived in Greenwich for many years, having previously sold another dwelling in the area for $2.7 million before relocating to their farmhouse.

They chose the farmhouse for its impressive parcel, noting to the outlet that they wanted more space for their horses.

However, they are now choosing to call to New York home.

Before settling down in Connecticut, Simms enjoyed a lengthy career in the NFL, a career that began at the University of Texas at Austin, after which he was drafted by the Buccaneers as the last pick of the final round in the 2003 NFL draft.

Simms remained with Tampa Bay until 2008, when he was released by the team. He was later picked up by the Tennessee Titans, with whom he played for a year before moving on to the Denver Broncos.

After a brief return to the Titans, the quarterback's career came to an end, with many pointing to a 2006 spleen injury as the reason for his retirement from the NFL.

He briefly tried his hand at coaching, signing with the New England Patriots in 2012 as an offensive coach, as well as a scouting expert, but he made a move into broadcasting after just a few months.

Simms and his wife, who met in high school, tied the knot in 2004 and now share two children.

#5696. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5695. Coinbase Brings ChatGPT Into Crypto Trading as Pancake Rebrand Signals Binance Rivalry

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Coinbase is bringing crypto trading directly into ChatGPT as competition for AI-powered financial services intensifies. Meanwhile, PancakeSwap has dropped “Swap” from its name, expanding beyond decentralized trading. The two developments show how Coinbase and Binance-linked crypto projects are positioning themselves for the next phase of digital finance.

Coinbase announced its ChatGPT integration yesterday, allowing users to connect accounts and manage portfolios. Users can check balances, analyze holdings, and place eligible trades using everyday language. And every order requires explicit approval before execution.

The timing coincides with Pancake’s attempt to reposition itself beyond its original decentralized exchange business.

Trade Base assets from ChatGPT@ChatGPT now connects to your Coinbase account, so you can trade Base assets in chat pic.twitter.com/tg9r2Iv3Qe

The Coinbase plugin allows eligible users to trade crypto and equities without leaving ChatGPT. Users can request market or limit orders through conversational instructions.

Before execution, ChatGPT displays an interactive confirmation card showing order details. Users must approve the transaction before Coinbase processes it through its Advanced Trade platform. Standard trading fees, eligibility requirements, and account limits still apply.

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong described the integration as another step toward an emerging agentic economy. The idea involves AI assistants handling increasingly complex financial tasks for users. But Coinbase still keeps humans responsible for approving individual trades for now.

To decentralize AI and preserve freedom, we need a coordination layer: a market economy where agents communicate and cooperate through prices.Teams of specialized open-weight models can outperform frontier models, just as a team of skilled people can outperform any single…

The integration also builds on Coinbase’s AI infrastructure. Its Coinbase for Agents toolkit provides developers with connections to trading accounts and market data. The ChatGPT launch brings those capabilities into a more accessible consumer interface.

As of today, the official integration currently remains limited to eligible U.S. Coinbase users. It also depends on ChatGPT account and workspace availability.

new brand, who dis?PancakeSwap is now Pancake 🥞6 years ago we were known for one thing. Today, we’re More Than a Swap. Let us reintroduce ourselves 👇 pic.twitter.com/J3P7Mocu2P

While Coinbase expands through ChatGPT, Pancake is changing how users perceive its decentralized trading ecosystem. Formerly known as PancakeSwap, the platform announced its rebrand today. The new identity reflects six years of expansion beyond its original token-swapping business.

Pancake now operates across more than 11 blockchain networks. The platform reports over 208 million users and more than $4.4 trillion in cumulative trading volume.

Its services now include perpetual contracts, tokenized stocks, ETFs, yield products, and developer infrastructure. The project is also preparing a dedicated mobile application. Its CAKE ticker and contract address remain unchanged, with existing staking positions unaffected.

Pancake’s relationship with Binance makes this rebrand interesting. Binance Labs announced a strategic investment in CAKE in June 2022. The investment supported the decentralized exchange’s development within the BNB Chain ecosystem.

The rivalry becomes clearer when looking beyond the latest announcements. Binance has already introduced its own AI infrastructure through Binance Agent OS. Launched in August 2026, the platform connects compatible AI applications with Binance trading, market data, wallet, and payment capabilities.

Its Model Context Protocol server supports compatible AI agents, including ChatGPT. Developers can build applications that access supported Binance services through user-controlled permissions.

Pancake is also developing its position in this emerging market. In July, the platform partnered with BNB Chain’s Agent Studio to help developers deploy autonomous agents.

These agents can interact with Pancake’s liquidity pools, rebalance positions, and execute trading strategies. Its AI tools also include portfolio planning and assistance across DeFi products.

This creates an interesting contrast between the two ecosystems. Coinbase is bringing AI-powered trading directly to consumers through ChatGPT. Binance is building infrastructure that allows developers and AI agents to interact with its services. Pancake adds a decentralized execution layer to the wider BNB Chain ecosystem.

The next battle in crypto may not be about which exchange attracts the most human traders. It could be about which infrastructure becomes the preferred destination for AI-powered financial activity.
